item.title: The Shadow of Yalta Hangs Over Trump’s Summit in China
item.description:
As the Second World War neared an end, the soon-to-be victors — Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union, Winston Churchill of Britain and President Franklin D. Roosevelt — sat down in the Crimean resort of Yalta to discuss the fate of postwar Europe. Their decisions in February 1945 helped shape the global order for the rest of the 20th century, making Yalta synonymous with an era of great-power bargaining by outsize personalities.

On Thursday, the leaders of the world’s three largest military powers will meet again. This time it will be President Xi Jinping of China, whose nation has supplanted Britain in military might, hosting President Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China — at an uncertain geopolitical moment dogged by wars, climate change and the rise of artificial intelligence — has prompted some analysts to label it “Yalta 2.0.”

That parallel has limits, historians say. For one, Yalta was a meeting of allies whose broad objectives overlapped, said Catherine Grace Katz, a historian of 20th century geopolitics and author of a book on that summit. “Or at least ostensibly still allies at the time,” she said.

By February 1945, the three Allied powers were united in their fight against Hitler’s Germany, whose defeat by then seemed inevitable. British and American troops had already stormed through France and Belgium, while the Soviet war machine was steamrolling across Eastern Europe, squeezing Germany from both flanks.

At Yalta, the allies agreed on what the Northern Hemisphere would look like after the dust of war settled.

Stalin agreed to join the fight against Japan in return for territory in the Northern Pacific. Roosevelt — by then frail, two months from his death and focused on ensuring Japan’s surrender — offered the Soviets broad leeway over Poland’s future. That set the stage for decades of Soviet domination over Eastern Europe.

David Reynolds, a professor of history at the University of Cambridge who specializes in 20th-century diplomacy, argued against overstating what was decided at Yalta.

“‘Yalta’ is a notorious word” that to many conjures the carving up of Europe and selling out to Stalin — but that is based on a misunderstanding, he said.

“The fate of postwar Europe was decided on the battlefield, not at the conference table,” he added.

By the time of the February conference, the Red Army was on the verge of taking Berlin, and both Roosevelt and Churchill had privately conceded the inevitability of Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, Professor Reynolds said.

Ms. Katz said, “Short of physically pushing them out of Poland, there was not a lot that the West could do.”

She also pointed out that it was a year earlier, at a meeting in Moscow, when Churchill and Stalin scribbled out their secret “percentages” agreement on a piece of paper. That led to Europe being split between Western and Communist blocs, a division that eventually became the Iron Curtain and persisted until the end of the Cold War.

Yalta was “not the moment that the world was carved up into these spheres of influence,” she said. “That kind of gets conflated with some of the other meetings that these wartime leaders had.”

That said, she argued, Roosevelt missed opportunities to press for greater concessions from Stalin at Yalta. The president took Stalin at his word when he insisted Poland's leaders couldn’t attend the conference, she said, and dismissed Churchill for being overly concerned with Poland’s future.

“Roosevelt was woefully unprepared in dealing with Stalin and understanding Russian history and Stalin’s true objectives when it came to Poland,” Ms. Katz said. (Successive U.S. administrations would similarly underestimate Moscow’s commitment to maintaining sway over Eastern Europe, culminating in Mr. Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.)

Professor Reynolds said that several other critical negotiations were also hammered out at Yalta, which is often forgotten.

It was the scene of hard-fought bargaining by Churchill to secure protections to stop Germany from being eviscerated under a future surrender, as Stalin had wanted, he said. Churchill was adamant that Europe needed to avert a disastrous repeat of the Treaty of Versailles at the end of the First World War, the terms of which were so punitive on Germany that many believe it planted the seeds of World War II.

“It is not the purpose of the Allies to destroy the people of Germany, or leave them without the necessary means of subsistence,” Churchill told British lawmakers in February 1945, after he had returned to London from Yalta. “Our policy is not revenge; it is to take such measures as may be necessary to secure the future peace and safety of the world.”

Roosevelt also used the Yalta conference to advance his blueprint for a new multilateral institution that would try to resolve conflicts through deliberation rather than war: the United Nations. It was formally established nine months later.

In other words, the suggestion that Yalta was synonymous with Europe’s “carve-up” by great powers flattens the history of the war’s final years, Professor Reynolds argued. “These historical events have a memory life, and all the other aspects that don’t fit within the memory narrative get forgotten,” he said.

item.title: ‘Shocking’ Signs of Climate Change Add Urgency to Latest U.N. Talks
item.description:
Chestnut trees in England that normally bloom in April are flowering in November. Whale sharks that typically stay in tropical waters are swimming off the California coast. And in Zimbabwe, rains that sustain the country’s agriculture have yet to arrive, leading to a drought that is threatening the food supply.

As negotiations continue this week in Turkey at the United Nations climate conference, diplomats and scientists there are confronting a planet where warning signs are flashing. From the Arctic to the tropics, unusual weather and extreme heat is sparking worry about how quickly humans are reshaping the Earth’s natural processes.

“Everything that scientists were warning about is happening,” said Rachel Cleetus, director of the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “We’re profoundly changing the planet for every life form that exists. It just feels like we’re letting the whole thing break before our eyes.”

At the start of the 12-day climate summit, which runs until Friday, world leaders detailed how climate change was wreaking havoc in their countries. Their top ministers are negotiating over ways to try to constrain global warming.

At the same time, leaders of the biggest polluting nations, President Trump, President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia were set to meet in Shenzhen, China, where climate change is not expected to be discussed. (The United States did not send a delegation to COP31.)

Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit. Just 11 years later, that goal is effectively dead. Scientists say that without drastic efforts to cut carbon emissions, the planet will likely warm at least 2.6 degrees Celsius, or 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels by the end of the century.

For those gathered at the U.N. climate conference, known as COP31, there was growing alarm that the effects of human-caused global warming were spiraling out of control.

“The climate crisis has not gone away, in fact it’s worsened,” said Chris Bowen, minister for climate change and energy for Australia, who is leading the negotiations in Turkey. “Countries around the world are dealing with natural disasters which are no longer natural, and dealing with impacts they never thought they would have to deal with.”

Fueling much of the extreme weather at the moment is an extraordinarily powerful El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by intense warming in an area of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean.

In recent weeks, waves of more than 50 feet driven by El Niño have crashed into the West Coast, which is also bracing for atmospheric rivers that are expected to dump record amounts of rain on California.

Near Peru, the waters are so warm that the country’s anchovy harvest has collapsed. Tropical fish are following warmer waters far from their usual habitat. In addition to the whale sharks off Malibu, there have been rare sightings of juvenile garibaldi fish in Monterey Bay, Calif.

According to Copernicus, Europe’s climate agency, ocean temperatures in August were the highest in recorded history.

“It’s shocking to see sea surface temperatures go completely off the charts,” said Johan Rockström, a Swedish scientist who is the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. “If this new rate of warming is the new normal, that would be very scary.”

The heat is also leading to unseasonable foliage worldwide. In Chile, the Atacama Desert is covered with wildflowers after rains from El Niño. And in England, an unusually warm autumn led chestnut trees to flower six months early.

Research published earlier this year found that even after accounting for other phenomena such as volcanic eruptions, solar radiation and natural variability, the rate of global warming has accelerated since 2015.

If global warming is speeding up, that means the worst effects of an overheated planet could arrive sooner than expected.

“It’s become clear that the consensus-based scientific process has vastly underestimated the speed and severity of climate impacts,” said Páll Gunnarsson, executive director of the Reykjavík Institute, a research organization in Iceland focused on climate tipping points. “What we’ve been seeing in the past few years goes way beyond what the models predicted.”

Last week, the polar vortex that usually keeps cold air trapped above the North Pole weakened unexpectedly, sending frigid air south. It is the earliest such event on record, and yet another sign that the planet’s natural systems may be out of whack.

Recent studies suggest that a powerful ocean current, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, that pulls heat up to Northern Europe could be at risk of breaking down.

“We find ourselves now facing a very credible threat,” Mr. Gunnarsson said of the potential of major changes to the current. “The more pessimistic scenarios are becoming more likely.”

Mr. Rockström said he worried that the planet was losing its ability to manage the additional heat trapped in the atmosphere by the relentless release of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels.

“With the acceleration of warming, the massive jump in heat levels in the ocean, the collapse of coral reef systems, I fear that we are moving toward a point where the biosphere is reaching a saturation point, where there’s a gradual decline in Earth’s capacity to absorb carbon,” he said.

item.title: Russia Vows to Rebuild Destroyed Crimea Bridge. It Could Take Years.
item.description:
Russian officials on Wednesday vowed to restore “within a tight time frame” the only bridge linking mainland Russia with Crimea after an elaborate Ukrainian attack knocked out its main roadway span. But restoration work is likely to take years.

It was the fourth time since Russia’s all-out invasion in 2022 that Ukraine managed to strike the structure, which is both symbolically and logistically important. After those earlier attacks, repairs took months. This time, the damage is far more extensive. Some Ukrainian officials questioned whether rebuilding would be possible at all with the threat of further attacks.

The steel arch that crashed into the sea early Tuesday after a Ukrainian drone and missile attack was the most complex element of the structure, known as the Kerch Strait Bridge.

Perched over a shipping channel, the nearly 750-foot-long arch was installed in October 2017, three years after Russia illegally annexed Crimea. It elevated the roadway more than 100 feet above the channel so cargo ships and other vessels could pass between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

The steel components were produced over several months at a factory in the Russian city of Voronezh. They were then welded together over roughly 11 months on a coastal slipway near the strait before being floated out on catamaran pontoons. It took several more months to connect the arch to the rest of the bridge and pave a road across it.

Andreas Kappos, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said that “about two years is a reasonable time for restoring traffic on the road bridge.” But that’s only if construction is not interrupted by Ukrainian strikes and if the piers supporting the arch span were not seriously damaged, he said.

Donald O. Dusenberry, a consulting engineer who has investigated bridge failures, said that simply clearing the debris would be a complicated job. He also noted that the single arch span was not like the repeatable spans that made up a majority of the bridge and could be fairly easily replaced. And if the piers must be repaired, that would add yet another layer of complication, he said.

Even so, Russia is likely to pour substantial resources into the reconstruction, given its significance to President Vladimir V. Putin and his government.

On Wednesday, Russia dispatched vessels, including one that could be used to clear debris, to the site of the attack, according to VesselFinder, a ship-tracking service.

The $4 billion bridge is a symbol of what Russia calls its “irreversible” control over Crimea. More broadly, it is a monument to Mr. Putin’s ambitions.

The Russian leader has linked his own image to the bridge, personally opening the roadway in May 2018 by driving a construction truck across it.

That was only part of the fanfare. A contest chose the bridge’s “official song” from more than 2,500 submissions, according to organizers. A feature film portrayed a love triangle against the backdrop of its construction. Russian pop stars performed at a concert marking its completion. The Russian central bank minted a special coin depicting the two main steel arches, and the Russian postal service issued a stamp celebrating the opening.

The bridge has become an equally potent symbol for Ukraine. In 2022, after Ukrainian forces struck the bridge for the first time, crowds lined up in Kyiv to buy their own postage stamp — one depicting the bridge in flames.

When it was built, the roadway bridge — together with a parallel railway bridge that remains open — provided the only direct land link between Russia and Crimea.

After the full-scale invasion in 2022, Russian troops captured a major overland highway linking Russia with Crimea. Over the past few years, Moscow has expanded the highway, restored damaged railways in the region and built new rail lines running to Crimea.

But compared with the bridge, those routes lie closer to the front line, making them more vulnerable to Ukrainian drone strikes. Last summer, Ukraine ramped up such attacks, disrupting traffic along the highway.

The roadway of the Kerch Strait Bridge has been a vital route for residents of Crimea and mainland Russia who traveled for tourism. Many Crimeans also drove across it to buy cheaper groceries in Russia’s neighboring Krasnodar region.

The bridge was used less often to supply the Russian war effort, military analysts said. Russia had curtailed its use for that purpose after the earlier Ukrainian attacks.

In October 2022, an explosion caused two sections of the road span to collapse and set fuel tankers ablaze on the parallel railway. It took Russia roughly four and a half months to reopen the highway and nearly seven months to complete repairs on the railway.

In July 2023, a Ukrainian naval drone attack caused one section to collapse and knocked another loose. It took Russia nearly three months to restore full traffic on the bridge.

Marc Santora contributed reporting.

item.title: Colombia Rejects Joint Plan With U.S. to Target Drug Gangs
item.description:
In a major setback for the Trump administration’s campaign against drug gangs, Colombia’s president has rejected a plan to allow the United States to conduct joint military operations in his country, according to U.S. officials.

The right-wing Colombian leader, Abelardo De La Espriella told Washington this week that though he supported working with the Pentagon to target drug organizations, he lacked the votes in Congress to approve such action, the officials said.

The officials requested anonymity to discuss a sensitive diplomatic matter.

Colombia has been key to the Pentagon’s plans to expand military operations across Latin America because it is one of the region’s biggest nations and has one of its most sophisticated military forces.

When Mr. De La Espriella came to power this year, he aligned himself with President Trump, promising a tough approach to drug groups and a crackdown on the violence prevalent in many regions of Colombia.

Colombia’s decision prompted the American defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to alter the four-country trip he is now making to Latin America.

Originally, he had been expected to meet on Wednesday with Colombian officials in Bogotá, the capital, to discuss the bilateral military agreement.

Instead, Mr. Hegseth was expected to touch down briefly to meet with Colombian officials after stopping in Caracas, Venezuela, where he met with the acting president and other officials. The defense secretary and the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, signed an agreement that Mr. Hegseth described as part of an “increased defense partnership.”

The military agreement with Colombia, known as Title 10, would have enabled U.S. forces to operate in that country and carry out joint airstrikes and ground operations.

Despite the setback, cooperation between the two countries remains strong. The United States and Colombia recently completed a major training exercise. And last week, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, met in Bogotá with top Colombia military leaders.

The Pentagon declined to comment on the matter. The White House and Colombia’s government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Hegseth was also expected to visit Ecuador, whose conservative president has already said he would allow joint military operations with the United States in his country.

Venezuelan and U.S. officials have drawn closer since the American military seized its autocratic leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January. The New York Times reported that the United States assisted the Venezuelan military in a deadly drone strike on an armed group in Venezuelan territory, and that the Trump administration was negotiating an agreement that would lay the foundation for a potential long-term U.S. military presence in the country.

Mr. De La Espriella’s inability to deliver Colombian cooperation casts doubt on the Pentagon’s plans for the region and its Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, which was announced earlier this year. In March, President Trump met with right-leaning Latin American leaders in Florida, pledging to work together to “eradicate the criminal cartels plaguing our region.”

Central to Mr. Trump’s goal was persuading Latin American nations to allow joint operations inside their territories.

The strategy is an aggressive expansion of the Pentagon’s airstrikes on alleged drug boats leaving South America. Many legal experts say those strikes are illegal under international laws forbidding the targeting of civilians, even if they are committing a crime, unless they pose an immediate threat.

Aside from opposition in Colombia’s legislature, U.S. troops on Colombian soil could also face significant pushback from the public. Colombia has a highly experienced military, and many citizens are likely to consider such a move an affront to sovereignty.

“Since the boat strikes began, the Trump administration has signaled a desire for land strikes,” said Brian Finucane, a former State Department lawyer who specializes in the laws of war. “Colombia shows that even in countries where the presidents are supportive of Trump, they still face domestic political and legal constraints on US military actions in their territory,”

Mr. Finucane said, “It should be a reality check for the administration that, unlike with the boat strikes, they aren’t going to have a free hand to do strikes willy-nilly in the territory of other states.”

Julie Turkewitz contributed reporting from Bogotá, Colombia.

item.title: Undoing Brexit
item.description:
Brexit was one of the most seismic events in modern British history. It’s had political, cultural and, perhaps above all, economic ramifications. So it’s been striking that in recent years, few politicians have been willing to say much about Britain’s 2016 vote to leave the European Union. That includes those who campaigned in favor of leaving the E.U. and those who opposed it.

But that’s changing. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is talking about Brexit — a lot. Today, I write about why Britain seems to be restarting a conversation about its relationship with the E.U., and what that actually means for its future.

Andy Burnham wants a reset with the European Union.

This week, in his first major foreign policy speech since becoming prime minister, Burnham had one clear message for the dignitaries assembled before him: “The Brexit we were given has not worked.”

It’s not the first time he’s used strong language about Britain’s decision to leave the E.U. Addressing Parliament this fall, he listed it as one of Britain’s historic “wrong turns.”

At his party conference a few weeks later, he said, “Brexit has done more harm than good.” When pressed, he told journalists that every option for a reset with Europe needed to be on the table, including going “all the way” — that is, rejoining the union.

For now, the goals of a Britain-E.U. summit in Brussels tomorrow are more modest: The two sides are expected to talk about re-establishing ways for young people to move between Britain and the E.U. more freely, a deal on agricultural products and linking their emissions markets, among other topics.

But the bigger question hanging over this rapprochement is whether Britain could actually rejoin the E.U. in the future, a question no one has dared to go near for the past decade. If Burnham has broken that taboo, it’s both because the politics around Brexit have shifted as the economic costs have become increasingly undeniable, and because the world in which Britain voted to leave has changed.

But that doesn’t mean Brexit is about to be reversed any time soon.

A perilous new world

Brexit was complicated territory for both major parties from the start. It split the Conservatives between those who wanted to stay in Europe’s single market and those who wanted to leave in the name of sovereignty and immigration control. It also divided Labour, whose educated and younger urban voters supported staying in, and whose traditional working-class base did not.

The 10 years since the vote have been messy. Six prime ministers have struggled to navigate Brexit’s aftermath, and essentially no major politicians have seen it in their interest to talk about it much.

But recently, a few things have changed, said Anand Menon, a professor at King’s College London who also spent a decade as the head of a think tank studying the relationship between Britain and Europe.

A consensus has more or less taken hold in Britain that Brexit was a bad idea. Two in three Britons now consider Brexit more of a failure than a success, polls show. It cost the economy 2 to 6 percent of G.D.P., according to a recent report, while not succeeding in lowering immigration. In fact, immigration from outside the E.U. has gone up.

But it’s not just that Brexit has hurt Britain’s economy. It’s that the economic case some Brexiteers once made no longer makes sense, if it ever did.

The referendum took place in a very different world from the one we live in now — before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine; before Donald Trump’s trade wars; before the Iran war.

The vision one camp of Brexiteers painted, of Britain as a small, wealthy sovereign nation outside the E.U., signing lucrative trade agreements with the whole world — Singapore-on-Thames, as they called it — relied on a rules-based, free-trading global order. It was a stretch at the time, Menon said; today, it’s impossible to envision.

And so the politics around Brexit have evolved too.

The Tories are still divided, Menon said, and also on the wrong side of an increasingly unpopular policy. With a few exceptions, they’re still largely staying away from the Europe question.

But Labour strategists say the party has already lost all the Leave voters it seems likely to lose. Its voters are now overwhelmingly people who voted against Brexit and those too young to have voted in the 2016 referendum. A pro-European stance, some have argued, could help Labour attract back voters who defected to more left-leaning parties. It could also make it harder for the Conservatives to lure young, educated voters away.

Labour, in other words, finally looks as if it has more to gain than to lose from talking about Brexit again.

Easier said than undone

Even as Burnham is ready to declare Brexit a mistake, though, there’s no consensus on how to fix it.

Even if most Britons now wish they hadn’t left the E.U., it’s far from clear whether they would be prepared to rejoin when faced with the policies they rejected: paying billions of pounds into the E.U. budget every year, for instance.

In that sense, Menon said, “the poll numbers are soft.”

And even if Brexit did economic damage to Britain, there’s a danger in casting rejoining as any sort of magic bullet. Any deal would take years to negotiate and could be slow to bring many benefits. And even then it would be unlikely to turn Britain’s economy around on its own.

In the meantime, some worry that the politics that up until recently made Brexit untouchable could quickly turn toxic again. What was once the Leave campaign is already mobilizing, rebranding itself as Stay Out.

In a recent interview, David Cameron, the former Conservative prime minister who called the fateful referendum in a bid to bury divisions and settle the Europe issue for good, had some words of advice for Burnham: Don’t go there.

The meeting today between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will be the first time in history that the leaders of the United States, China and Russia — which have more than 90 percent of the world’s nuclear weapons — sit down together.

The three leaders want to project the image that they are guiding the world order, but they are unlikely to settle major issues during their talks in Shenzhen, China. Here’s the latest.

David Sanger, our White House and national security correspondent, explains in the video below what’s at stake when you put three leaders with vast powers, vast nuclear arsenals and big egos in the same room.

Some analysts are calling the meeting “Yalta 2.0” — comparing it to the conference between Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin at the end of World War II. But the parallel has limits.

But when Buckwalter asked for a copy of the data from his own brain, the researchers said no. That’s when things got complicated.

A senior conservator, she used tools for maintaining priceless artworks that could’ve been assembled from a household cleaning closet: dusters, sponges, brushes, rags, vacuums. item.title: Isolated Amazon Indigenous Group Makes Rare Contact
item.description:
Community members in a Brazilian village in the Amazon rainforest were astonished this week to see a group of isolated Indigenous people emerge from the brush and ask for food, government officials said.

On Monday morning, a group of Indigenous Awá people made rare contact with the villagers, according to a statement from Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples. The encounter raised fears that decades of illicit deforestation, cattle ranching and hunting have pushed the forest’s inhabitants to a breaking point.

It was the first time in recent memory that a group of Awá had willingly left their isolated lives to make contact, said Sarah Shenker, a campaigner at the Indigenous rights group, Survivor International.

“They’ve shown so clearly for so long that they don’t want contact with outsiders,” said Ms. Shenker, who has visited the area regularly since 2010. “So this moment is really alarming.”

Videos and images of the Awá, taken by community members and shared by Survivor International, a U.K.-based group, show adults and children huddled near the edge of the forest in the northeastern Brazilian state of Maranhão. Some are bearing necklaces and headdresses, or holding spears. In all, they numbered around 20, the right group said.

The Awá initially approached nearby officers from FUNAI, a government agency that supports Indigenous communities, officials said.

Communicating through gestures, the Awá asked for yams, which they brought back into the forest, Ms. Shenker said. Some members of the Awá group continued to come and go in the following days, she said.

The immediate concern was for their health, Ms. Shenker said.

Lacking both exposure to common pathogens and vaccinations, Ms. Shenker said, the Awá were vulnerable to any diseases they might catch from the Guajajara. That is a larger group of Indigenous people in Maranhão.

As images and videos of the encounter began to circulate on social media, Brazil’s Indigenous peoples ministry mobilized a response involving local and national health authorities.

“Brazilian policy for the protection of isolated Indigenous peoples is guided by the principle of non-contact,” the statement said. “Its objective is not to promote relations with these peoples, but to guarantee the necessary conditions for them to remain in isolation if that is their decision, without external interference and with full protection of their territories.”

For decades, wildfires, illicit logging, ranching and hunting have led to the destruction of Indigenous peoples’ livelihoods in the Amazon, Ms. Shenker said. The government has designated certain areas as protected Indigenous land, she said, but now, “this territory and a few other Indigenous territories in the region are the only places where valuable hardwoods still stand.”

About 15 years ago, the Guajajara people formed groups called the “Forest Guardians,” which confronted illegal logging camps and confiscated equipment, Ms. Shenker said at least six of them were killed while doing so, she said.

While some Awá people have chosen to make contact, Ms. Shenker said, about three or four subgroups reject contact with outsiders. The Awá move freely and survive entirely from the forest, she said, hunting wild boar, deer, monkeys and fish and gathering fruit and honey. They build shelters from tree fibers.

The forest is also their source of medicine and spirituality, she said.

Survivor International has not yet reached any conclusions about why the Awá emerged this week, but said it was troubling.

“The fact that they’ve come out now does indicate that they have probably felt forced to for one reason or another,” Ms. Shenker said. “And as we say, because their lives are so intricately related to the forest, it would be impossible to completely separate the pressures on the land.”

item.title: How We Broke Open the Nvidia Investigation
item.description:
“You stumble into stories like this once in your career.”

The Times reporter Tripp Mickle told me that the other day when we were discussing how, in the summer of 2025, he and his colleagues heard something that proved to be the beginning of a long reporting journey about the American tech company Nvidia, China and artificial intelligence chips. That work eventually drew in reporters across time zones and news desks, from Washington and Silicon Valley to Asia and Europe.

Last month, The Times revealed a Chinese spying plot on Nvidia, and the fallout led to the resignation of one of America’s leading executives, Jensen Huang of Nvidia.

I dug into the journey and decision-making this week with key reporters and editors who collaborated on the effort. These questions and answers have been lightly edited.

In October 2025, we published an article revealing the social interactions between Jensen Huang and a Singaporean data-center executive named Alice Huang — and how they were drawing interest from U.S. officials looking at whether her company was helping Chinese tech firms sidestep American export restrictions. Take us back to the moment when you realized there was potentially a story here.

TRIPP MICKLE, Silicon Valley reporter: Early August of 2025 was a big time in the world of semiconductors. Bigger than perhaps we could have appreciated. President Trump announced a deal to invest $8.9 billion in Intel. Jensen Huang said Nvidia was working on a “new product” for China. And we started to hear chatter in tech circles about a company that we’d never heard of called Megaspeed.

We knew about the phenomenon of Southeast Asian data centers that the U.S. government suspected were smuggling chips to China. Through our research, we found that this Singapore company had ties to Mr. Huang. He was in a photograph on LinkedIn seated at an industry party beside Alice Huang, who claimed to be Megaspeed’s chief executive officer.

The photograph, in many ways, encapsulated the story we’d spend the next year of our lives trying to tell.

ANA SWANSON, trade and international economics reporter: Yes — we were intrigued by Alice Huang’s seemingly close relationship with Jensen Huang. At the time, we uncovered photos and videos of them at that party in Taiwan in 2024 and another dinner where they seemed intimate in 2025.

We were also intrigued to discover that U.S. officials were pursuing an investigation into chip smuggling by the firm. We did a lot of Chinese-language research. The clincher for me is when we acquired trade records showing truly massive shipments of Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell technology going from California to Malaysia. Megaspeed was a previously unknown firm with close ties to China and Jensen Huang buying billions of dollars of the most sensitive American technology. It was a remarkable confluence of factors that in many ways remains the core of the story still today.

Three weeks ago, we published the revelation about the close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang: U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been funneling information to Beijing. Did you know what a huge impact this story would have?

MAGGIE HABERMAN, White House correspondent: We knew that we were covering a significant news story, with potentially major ramifications and ripple effects. Speaking for myself, I didn’t expect events to escalate so quickly. Our initial story about the U.S. intelligence agencies having electronic surveillance on Alice Huang published on Oct. 29. It was just several days later that we reported on the existence of a government memo describing the situation, followed by a story that it was drawn up by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

We know some people are focused on the salacious elements here, but the much larger and more durable issue is the possibility that banned, high-end Nvidia chips were smuggled into China.

JULIAN BARNES, intelligence and national security reporter: I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted. This was about a Chinese intelligence asset having a close relationship with the C.E.O. of one of the most important artificial intelligence companies on the planet. Perhaps it was Mr. Huang’s denials that anything was amiss in his interview with Bloomberg. But we followed other threads, like the fact that Alice Huang was working with China’s Ministry of State Security, according to multiple people who were briefed on the matter. And as we kept writing, Mr. Huang changed his story and the Nvidia board began its investigation.

This story reaches across continents and touches on some of the world’s most powerful people, including the president of the United States. What was key in wrapping your arms around that reporting effort?

JONATHAN SWAN, White House correspondent: When you get on a big, complicated story like this, you see the full power of The New York Times’s newsroom come to life. I know that sounds immodest, but we’re fortunate here and it’s worth saying it out loud. Never in my career, before joining The Times, could I have imagined being able to team up with reporters in Southeast Asia, Washington and Silicon Valley to chase down every new angle and lead. We each brought our own piece of the puzzle, and none of us could have delivered this reporting on our own. But we have a lot still to learn and many unanswered questions.

What changed most over the last 15 months about what we knew or were able to publish? In other words: What did it take to push the story from reporting that poses more questions than answers — literally posing the headline as a question: “A Mystery C.E.O. and Billions in Sales: Is China Buying Banned Nvidia Chips?” — into the headline three weeks ago about Jensen Huang being seen as a target of Chinese spying?

JONATHAN: Maggie and I had been hearing astonishing tips from sources that there was much more to understand about Jensen Huang and his interactions in Asia, well beyond what was in the public view. This information was a closely held secret inside the Trump administration. It took several months of digging but we ​and Julian finally got the break that there was a suspected Chinese intelligence asset who was in a relationship with the Nvidia chief executive. And the U.S. intelligence community had her under surveillance. The headline of our story, on Oct. 29, would read: “Nvidia Chief Seen as Target of Chinese Spy Plot.” Given Mr. Huang’s close relationship with President Trump, this brought the president and the White House right into the story.

PAUL MOZUR, global technology correspondent: In the first investigation, it was so clear there was so much more going on. There were empty offices and shell companies in Singapore. Then there was Alice, who clearly had the ear of Jensen. Putting it together took a lot of methodical effort. Ana and I would sometimes just get on the phone together to comb through thousands of records of microchip shipments. I’m still a bit stunned that our dive on this strangely named company in Singapore turned into what it has become. It shows you never know where the string will lead.

In various articles, we’ve described our sources as “people briefed on the surveillance” or “officials who had seen that intelligence.” You’re not going to reveal the identity of our sources, but can you talk generally about our approach to anonymous sourcing?

PUI-WING TAM, business editor: As much as possible, we want people to be on the record. But sometimes that is difficult if situations are sensitive. In general, we value people with firsthand information, and we aim to verify, verify, verify through other sources or documents for accuracy.

JULIAN: As a reporter who covers intelligence and national security, many of my stories are based on anonymous sources. Classification rules and leak hunts mean that people with knowledge of sensitive national security matters cannot speak for attribution without fear of losing their jobs or potential prosecution. The information behind this story — involving spies, intelligence collection, China and one of the most important American companies — was especially sensitive.

We realize that it is frustrating to readers when we cannot quote people by name. But it is important for readers to understand the care we take. Stories like these demand multiple sources, beyond a single source. We seek out multiple people with different perspectives or views. When we use anonymous sources, we know we are asking readers to trust The New York Times, and we never take that trust for granted.

Getting this story also involved a lot of old-fashioned shoe-leather reporting: tracking down documents, following the money, knocking on doors. We traced the purchase of billions of dollars of Nvidia technology by Megaspeed, the company that employed Alice Huang, and explored its murky origins and connections to China. Take us inside that effort.

PAUL: A year ago I went to Singapore to see what we could find on the ground about Megaspeed. I talked my way into their office building and to my great surprise, found a very helpful and slightly confused manager in the office who confirmed much of what we had suspected: All the executives were Chinese, and they rarely showed up in Singapore.

At times things turned darker. When I went to Malaysia to visit offices there, a Chinese man told me to leave the office alone. Then a team of three followed me around the shopping mall where the offices were. We still don’t know who the people were. I actually ended up putting photos and a description of the process on Instagram, because it reminded me so much of my time in China, when we were regularly tailed by Chinese security. It just showed, as a journalist you have to show up, because you never know what will happen.

TRIPP: While Paul was having his adventure in Singapore, I was driving around the asphalt flatlands of Silicon Valley. The reams of shipment data we gathered showed Megaspeed received chips from a half-dozen local addresses. I went to abandoned warehouses and offices in San Jose, Fremont and Milpitas. I talked to employees in the parking lot of one warehouse and watched through an open trucking bay as they loaded boxes of computing equipment on crates. Then I went to the business office of Aivres, Megaspeed’s primary supplier, which is an arm of a Chinese company blacklisted for funneling technology to Beijing’s military. Everyone at the office spoke Mandarin, and they shooed me away.

What made you feel ready to finally press “publish” on our scoop revealing Jensen Huang as the target of a Chinese spy plot?

RICHARD W. STEVENSON, Washington bureau chief: We were well aware of the impact the story would have and the scrutiny it would draw. We checked back with our sources repeatedly and examined the language in the story line by line to assure that we had solid reporting to back up every factual assertion. And we stress-tested our reporting from multiple angles to assure that our conclusions were consistent with all of the information we gathered. Only then did senior editors at The Times sign off on the story and give the go-ahead to publish.

Some critics of our reporting have recently argued that we have not definitively established that Alice Huang was a spy. We ourselves reported last week that U.S. intelligence agencies are still assessing when they believe Ms. Huang began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there. How can readers be sure that we have this right, especially when much of the reporting is based on anonymous sources?

RICHARD: We have full confidence in the accuracy of what we reported: that Alice Huang is believed by the U.S. government to have been a Chinese asset who was exploiting her relationship with Jensen Huang for intelligence purposes.

Relying on anonymous sources is never ideal, but sometimes it is the only way to surface information that is important to understanding what is happening inside the government. That is especially true when the subject matter involves national security and espionage, or involves powerful people who have the capacity for retribution. When we produce a story based largely or entirely on unnamed sources, we have a special responsibility to ensure that our information is confirmed by multiple people who have independent knowledge of the facts.

Taking a step back, why are the romantic entanglements of an executive like Jensen Huang newsworthy?

JIM YARDLEY, assistant managing editor for enterprise and investigations: It’s a good question, but in this case the answer is pretty compelling. The Times has reported on two cases in which Mr. Huang has had extramarital relationships. The first was with Alice Huang and raised clear issues: Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful American leaders in A.I., a man who has direct access to the president and helps shape White House policy on chips, was involved with a woman who U.S. officials concluded was passing information to Chinese intelligence. This raises national security concerns. And the Commerce Department was also investigating her company on whether it was illegally smuggling chips into China.

The second case involved Mr. Huang’s extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia, a woman who reported directly to him. This relationship violated the company’s own code of conduct, and after The Times first reported the relationship, the Nvidia board held an emergency meeting. Mr. Huang resigned the next day.

He has been among the world’s most powerful figures in promoting and guiding the A.I. revolution, and these incidents raised legitimate questions both about national security concerns but also about his judgment.

Some readers have been asking “why now” about this reporting. The question implies that this reporting is part of an organized conspiracy to depose Mr. Huang. How do you see the “why now” critique and other questions about the timing of what we published?

TRIPP: Anything this complex takes time. This was the culmination of a year of work and the doggedness and patience of a team that worked hard to make sense of a complicated business relationship and determinations of industrial espionage.

ANA: I totally agree, and I’d add that we have been consistently reporting on this topic for a long time. We published the original story about Alice Huang and her ties with Jensen in October 2025. In September of this year, we turned to one of Megaspeed’s main suppliers, the U.S. based subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm. We have been steadily pushing ahead with this reporting over time, and it’s only now that it has exploded into popular consciousness, for reasons largely outside our control.

JONATHAN: We published when we had confidence in the information and when the story was ready to be published. The same way we do with any story.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
President Trump is expected to sit down with Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in China on Thursday, concluding his whirlwind Asian trip with a three-way summit in which he may discuss nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine with the authoritarian leaders.

The meeting in the city of Shenzhen, a metropolis just north of Hong Kong, will be the first of its kind between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States. Officials who planned the trip have cautioned that they do not expect major breakthroughs or agreements. But that seems beside the point for the three men, who all seem intent on projecting their power.

Mr. Trump will also meet separately with both leaders in Shenzhen, which is hosting a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a group of 21 economies. As APEC leaders gathered on Thursday morning, Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin warmly shook hands with each other as they took their positions for a group photo before attending a meeting.

With Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump is seeking to reassert American leadership in artificial intelligence and to pin the Chinese leader down on extending a trade truce that is set to expire in January. The president also hopes to persuade Mr. Xi to continue to allow shipments of rare earths and magnets to the United States.

With Mr. Putin, the American president intends to discuss the war in Ukraine. He has not seen the Russian leader in person since August 2025, when Mr. Trump hosted him for a bilateral meeting in Alaska. Mr. Trump left the meeting with only a promise of a later agreement on the war that has not materialized.

Mr. Putin has been under increasing pressure to resolve the war in Ukraine, which has weakened his country’s economy and caused high Russian casualties. Still, he has shown little inclination to end the invasion, and is expected to keep fighting at least through the winter, according to Western intelligence assessments.

For his part, Mr. Xi may hope that the three-way meeting in China symbolizes a leveling of global power, a shift to a future where the United States is not the dominant player. He is expected to telegraph his close relationship with Mr. Putin while extending a flattering welcome to Mr. Trump, who is known to enjoy the ceremonial trappings of power. Mr. Xi also wants to show off the city of Shenzhen, a software and robotics hub.

On nuclear weapons, Mr. Trump is prepared to talk about Beijing’s growing arsenal with Mr. Xi, his advisers said, though it is a topic the Chinese are reluctant to discuss. China is on track to have 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030, producing them at a pace that has worried U.S. officials and analysts.

Here’s what else to know:

A.I. race: Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump both spoke about A.I. in their remarks at the APEC meeting. The Chinese leader called on the group to build an “open ecosystem” for the technology, a notable comment given the competition for A.I. supremacy between his country and the United States. Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech that he opposed A.I. regulation that would stifle growth.

Song choice: World leaders were welcomed with fanfare by Chinese musicians at a banquet on Wednesday. For Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan, the band played a song inspired partly by postwar protests against the U.S. military presence in her country. Was it a message to a close American ally? Read more ›

Yalta’s shadow: It appears unlikely that the trilateral meeting will live up to the comparisons to the conference in Yalta, where Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met toward the end of World War II to divide up the globe. Read more ›

item.title: India is not in the room in Shenzhen, but it’s watching closely.
item.description:
When the leaders of China, Russia and the United States meet in Shenzhen on Thursday, India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, will not be in the room.

But India will have much at stake in the gathering.

Russia and the United States are among India’s most crucial economic partners. China is arguably its most important rival. How the leaders of the three countries get along when they meet, and any deals they might make, will have important consequences for New Delhi.

First, any discussion of the war in Iran affects India enormously. Skyrocketing energy prices have battered India, which depends on the Strait of Hormuz — which has been blocked for months — for much of its oil and gas imports. India relies on remittances from millions of workers in the Persian Gulf, and several of its sailors on commercial vessels have been killed or injured amid the war in Iran.

Second, the war between Russia and Ukraine has choked the supply of food and energy across the Black Sea and threatened Indian seafarers in that shipping corridor.

Third, India’s trade relations with both China and the United States are not great. India and the Trump administration have been working on a trade deal for months, but with little to show for it. So last year’s tariffs on India remain in place. India has ambitions to expand its renewable energy infrastructure in the face of high oil and gas prices, but to do that it depends largely on imports of materials and equipment from China.

The Indian Express newspaper this week urged Indian officials to “push for a stable order.”

The meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will almost certainly have repercussions for India’s economy and security. But India will not be there to influence the outcome.

item.title: A Hunt for Test Cheats With Phone Alerts and Eyeglasses Checks
item.description:
At 8:30 a.m. on Thursday every phone in South Korea buzzed loudly, even the ones set on silent. It was an emergency alert sent by the government, the kind usually reserved for a natural disaster or wartime catastrophe.

But this alert was designed to sniff out would-be cheaters taking a test that is held every November.

The exam, the eight-hour College Scholastic Ability Test, or Suneung, is notoriously grueling and has spawned the country’s cram school culture. Last year’s edition had an English comprehension section so difficult that it prompted an apology from administrators and a resignation. This year, the authorities are worried about students cutting corners, given an alarming rise of A.I.-assisted chicanery.

On Tuesday, just two days before the Suneung, they announced a host of new rules.

Test takers — more than half a million this year — were ordered to roll up their sleeves. They had to put stickers on their shirt and jacket buttons, blinding any cameras they might have hidden in them. For the same reason, they had to let proctors inspect their eyeglasses. The emergency alert was expected to sound off again at least once during the exam, which started at 8:40 a.m.

The rhythms of life in South Korea change on the day of the test, which is held on the third Thursday of November. Traffic restrictions are put in place around test centers, people delay their commutes and flights are grounded for 35 minutes during the listening portion of the test.

Many students and their parents see the new security measures as a last-minute disruption.

“An alarm would completely disrupt my flow,” a test taker told local news media. “The Korean language portion is all based on flow.” Some even called to postpone the exam until more formal and foolproof measures had been established. Previous changes to test questions and protocol have elicited a similar response.

The test, which is also known as CSAT, is divided into six sections that test students on subjects like English, math, and history. But the questions are not as straightforward as the subjects seem. Past exams had students solving questions about equity capital, risk-weighted bank assets and Piaget’s theory of cognitive development.

Officials defended the last-minute changes, saying they were necessary in wake of recent scandals. “Cheating on exams using high-tech equipment is nothing less than outright theft,” President Lee Jae Myung said on social media on Tuesday. He offered a bounty of at least 100 million won, about $75,000, to informers, who will get more money the more people they report.

Last month, several students were caught cheating with smart glasses in admissions exams for Yonsei University and the University of Seoul, according to lawmakers. Earlier this month, a student at Konkuk University, was caught attempting to use a mini camera in a mock exam, according to local news media.

On Nov. 15, a man named Han Won-seok, who received the top score in a certified tax accountant exam, confessed to using A.I. to cheat on the test. In a YouTube video on his lawyer’s channel, Mr. Han said he used a mini camera to take pictures of the test which were uploaded to a cloud-based generative A.I. service that solved the questions for him. He received the answers using a hidden phone.

“To anyone who might be contemplating cheating like I did,” Mr. Han said, “please, do not hold onto the reckless thought of ‘maybe I won’t get caught.’”

Anyone caught using A.I. to cheat on the college entrance exam will face a 10-year ban from retaking it and possible criminal charges. The government said it would work with A.I. companies after the exam to check for test queries during test hours but did not identify them.

item.title: Florida Man Found Guilty in Plot to Kill Haiti’s President
item.description:
A Haitian American man was convicted in Florida on Wednesday in a wide-ranging conspiracy to kidnap or kill the last elected president of Haiti, Jovenel Moïse, in 2021. The subsequent assassination plunged the impoverished country into chaos.

A federal jury in Miami convicted the man, Christian Emmanuel Sanon, of all eight counts against him, including providing material support and leading a military expedition against a foreign country. Mr. Sanon could now face life in prison. His sentencing was scheduled for February.

Zeljka Bozanic, one of Mr. Sanon’s lawyers, said by phone that an appeal was planned. “We respect the jury’s decision, but we strongly disagree with it,” Ms. Bozanic said.

Mr. Sanon, 67, who has dual nationality, had said he was a doctor and pastor, but there is no record of his having a U.S. medical degree or leading a church.

The married father of three from South Florida was the 11th defendant to be convicted in the case, in which more than 40 people have been charged. Four South Florida men were found guilty in a separate trial in May by a federal jury in Miami of conspiring in Mr. Moïse’s assassination.

Throughout the nearly eight-week trial in Miami, Mr. Sanon had maintained his innocence. He testified in his own defense last week that he loved Haiti, the country of his birth, and wanted to find a way to replace a president he believed was shredding Haiti’s democracy.

In making plans to become Haiti’s president, he had boasted that he had the backing of the U.S. government, prosecutors said. They accused Mr. Sanon of teaming with a South Florida security firm and a hit squad of Colombian former military commandos, who stormed Mr. Moïse’s presidential residence at night. Mr. Moïse was shot at point-blank range in his bedroom in the middle of the night with his wife by his side.

Mr. Sanon’s defense painted him as a naïve and trusting family man who became a pawn in a large multinational plot that he did not believe would end in an assassination.

Ms. Bozanic told the jury that the mountain of evidence in the case, including thousands of text messages between the conspirators, failed “to show that Mr. Sanon had any knowledge of what the ultimate conspiracy to kidnap or kill the president would be.”

Federal prosecutors, however, described him as a con man with a “lust for power” who posed as an opposition leader with influential friends in the U.S. government that he did not have. Assistant U.S. Attorney Altanese Phenelus used the text messages and documents to argue that Mr. Sanon had been an integral part of the plot and often referred in messaged to “we” and “us.”

Mr. Sanon testified that the original plan was to oust Mr. Moïse by fomenting a popular uprising. Mr. Sanon, who has no political experience, would have then seized power and have Mr. Moïse arrested. In 2021, Mr. Sanon enlisted a small Miami security firm, Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy, in his plans, according to court documents. The firm raised money to pay for weapons, gear and the Colombian mercenaries, prosecutors said.

When the original plan failed to materialize, Mr. Sanon was dropped by the conspirators, who chose a former Haitian Supreme Court justice, Wendelle Coq, to replace Mr. Moïse, prosecutors said. Although Mr. Moïse was killed, their plan to install Ms. Coq quickly collapsed after they were surrounded by the Haitian police and arrested. Three of the Colombians were killed in a shootout.

Mr. Moïse had presided over a country buffeted by instability, endemic corruption and gang violence. Mr. Moïse, who won the 2016 elections, in the last months of his tenure had embarked on a constitutional redraft that would have let the president run for two consecutive terms. His refusal to cede power had angered many Haitians.

Haiti has not had a president since the killing of Mr. Moïse, whose death became a symbol of the poor Caribbean nation’s descent into mayhem. Haiti has been run on an interim basis by a series of unelected prime ministers and a Presidential Transitional Council, with no sitting Parliament. The council’s mandate ended in February.

The assassination of Mr. Moïse led to a power vacuum in Haiti, where armed gangs have seized control of most of the capital, Port-au-Prince, leading to the intervention of a United Nations-backed foreign military gang-suppression force, as well as more than 2,000 soldiers from El Salvador.

His widow, Martine Moïse, who was wounded in the assassination, has registered to run for president in an election that, for now, is scheduled for next year.

item.title: Was China Sending a Musical Message to Japan’s Leader?
item.description:
As they arrived for a banquet in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, world leaders were welcomed with fanfares by Chinese musicians. They played “America the Beautiful” for President Trump, the folk song “Cielito Lindo” for President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico and the traditional ballad “Drifting Ferns, Floating Clouds” for Vietnam’s leader, To Lam.

When Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, entered the hall, the band offered a more unconventional choice: “Ue o Muite Arukou,” also known as “Sukiyaki.” The song, which was released in 1961 and became a global hit, was inspired partly by protests against the U.S. military presence in Japan after World War II.

Was China, which has been locked in a bitter political feud with Japan for a year, trying to send a musical message to Ms. Takaichi, a defense hawk and close American ally?

“It’s only natural to suspect that the choice of song was carefully choreographed,” said Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington and a former foreign correspondent for Nikkei.

The point, he added, was clear: “A song rooted in opposition to the U.S.-Japan alliance, being played to welcome a Japanese prime minister in China.”

China has been at odds with Japan since last year, when Ms. Takaichi suggested that Japan could be forced to get involved militarily in case of a Chinese attack on Taiwan. Beijing considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy, part of its territory.

The Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, has since attempted to drive a wedge between Ms. Takaichi and her allies, including Mr. Trump. In speeches, diplomatic talks and propaganda, Mr. Xi’s government has tried to portray Japan as an aggressor and a resurgent military power that cannot be trusted.

Ms. Takaichi has seemed eager to make the most of the forum in Shenzhen, despite some signs of frostiness. While other leaders were greeted by cheering crowds at the airport in Shenzhen, she received a far more subdued welcome on the tarmac.

Ms. Takaichi briefly met Mr. Xi before the banquet — their first encounter in more than a year — but he did not appear to respond when she tried to engage him in conversation. The two leaders shook hands and posed for a photo.

On Thursday, Ms. Takaichi appeared to have a lot to say to Mr. Xi when they met again before the day’s discussions. It was unclear what she told him, but Mr. Xi nodded and offered a slight smile.

For her part, Ms. Takaichi, an amateur heavy metal drummer, appeared pleased by the rendition of “Ue o Muite Arukou.” She smiled and bowed her head to the musicians.

“Ue o Muite Arukou,” which was sung by Kyu Sakamoto, with lyrics by Ei Rokusuke, was the only Japanese-language song to reach the top of the Billboard Hot 100 chart in 1963. The title translates roughly as “I Walk Looking Up.”

Mr. Ei has written that the song was about the “sense of defeat” he felt at the time about negotiations over a security treaty with the United States. He had taken part in protests opposing the treaty.

The song itself does not directly speak about protest or war, but describes feelings of loneliness and heartbreak:

I look up as I walk

So that the tears won’t fall

But the tears well up as I walk

For tonight, I am all alone

Kiuko Notoya and Hisako Ueno contributed reporting.

item.title: How to Decode the Xi-Trump Hug
item.description:
Around three thousand years ago, the kings of Babylon and Assyria shook hands to cement an alliance. We know that because a sculptor carved the moment into limestone, and the work is now on display in a Iraqi museum.

The artifact helps us measure how long world leaders have been making the same gestures of respect, and how long the rest of us have been scrutinizing the slightest differences in their body language. We read volumes into the placement of a hand, let alone subtle deviations from tradition, which is what the world saw on Wednesday when President Trump and China’s leader Xi Jinping embraced each other briefly, ahead of a series of meetings.

Mr. Xi’s presence on the tarmac as Mr. Trump descended from Air Force One in China alone was already a break with decades of diplomatic custom, under which lower-ranking officials are generally sent to welcome visiting heads of state.

China’s state-run news agency reported that Mr. Xi was reciprocating Mr. Trump’s mold-breaking decision to greet Mr. Xi in person when he arrived at Andrews Air Force Base for a state visit to the United States in May.

The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are clearly trying to signal closeness at a time when the entire world seems increasingly fractious, and when relations between their two nations are strained over several tough issues, including trade barriers, nuclear arms control and the artificial intelligence race.

“This gesture likely reflects Xi and Beijing’s desire to show respect to Trump, which they know the U.S. President enjoys,” William Yang, a senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, wrote in a social media post. “And it is likely also an attempt to uphold the positive rapport between Xi and Trump ahead of a potentially turbulent period in U.S.-China relations in the coming months.”

Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump will be joined by the Russian president, Vladimir V. Putin, for three-way talks on Thursday, the first trilateral meeting of its kind. Mr. Putin, who has met Mr. Xi dozens of times, was greeted not by Mr. Xi but by Cai Qi, a member of China’s Politburo Standing Committee.

All of this is being dissected by the media and by historians, just as these leaders’ past gestures have been. In 2017, The Times brought on two experts in body language to analyze Mr. Trump’s handshakes with various world leaders after a string of awkward interactions provided ample fodder for speculation about the geopolitical meanings behind his etiquette.

A mangled handshake with French president Emmanuel Macron was “very patronizing,” remarked Jacqueline Whitmore, an author and etiquette instructor. Mr. Trump’s missed cue to shake hands with the German chancellor at the time, Angela Merkel, signaled he was “disinterested,” said Chris Ulrich, who teaches body language and presentation skills.

But Mr. Trump hit the mark with a strong face-to-face handshake with Canada’s prime minister, Justin Trudeau, in 2017, Mr. Ulrich said. It wasn’t just that they made sustained eye contact or touched each other’s left arms. “You face your belly button toward people you like, admire and trust,” he said. “This is a great way to build rapport fast.”

In Shenzhen, where Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin have planned their trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of a larger gathering of leaders for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, the differences in greetings were clearer.

Mr. Xi’s personal welcome of Mr. Trump appeared to reflect a desire for a measure of stability despite a growing disagreements. And the more conventional reception for Mr. Putin by one of Mr. Xi’s underlings signaled a kind of continuity in relations between China and Russia.

In contrast, Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, was practically shunned by Mr. Xi when she arrived in Shenzhen.

Relations between Japan and China are at their lowest point in decades, and Ms. Takaichi was greeted when she arrived not by a top minister, but by military guards and a woman whom Japanese media said was the Chinese foreign ministry’s ambassador of protocol.

Later, at the hall where the forum was taking place, Mr. Xi barely took note of Ms. Takaichi. He offered her only a slight smile as she made her way to a banquet with other world leaders, and he did not appear to respond when she said a few words to him, just before they posed for a photo.

item.title: How the War in Iran Will Remake the Global Energy Order
item.description:
When the United States and Israel went to war against Iran, restricting access to a fifth of the world’s oil and much of its gas through the Strait of Hormuz, Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency, called the market disruption the greatest threat to global energy security ever.

On Thursday, nearly nine months into the conflict, Mr. Birol and the I.E.A. declared that the upheaval has permanently reshaped the world’s energy system.

In its most thorough assessment yet of the war’s impact on energy, the agency found that the conflict has accelerated a shift toward electrification and domestic power generation. The war in Iran has shattered the Strait of Hormuz’s reputation as a reliable energy corridor — making a return to prewar conditions unlikely despite a recent recovery in Persian Gulf oil exports.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” Mr. Birol said in a statement accompanying the agency’s World Energy Outlook report.

The I.E.A., based in Paris, is a multinational organization that conducts extensive research on energy and advises member nations on policies. The agency was established as a counterweight to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, or OPEC, after the oil shock caused by the 1973-74 Arab oil embargo.

The findings come as diplomats from nearly 200 nations gather in Antalya, Turkey, for annual United Nations climate talks. Many are focused on trying to ensure that the war-induced pivot toward electrification and homegrown energy leads to a transition away from fossil fuels. Several participants at the talks, known as COP31, said moving more swiftly to electrification could be the best chance of getting the world back on track to keeping the rise in global temperatures to relatively safe levels.

The report is not a light read. Across 563 pages, the I.E.A. games out different scenarios for how nations are responding to the Gulf crisis now and how they might in the future.

“Previous energy shocks, from the 1970s onwards, all left lasting marks on the energy world,” the report states, adding, “This one will too, and the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper these marks will be.”

None of those scenarios, they stressed, should be considered a definitive prediction.

On one end of the spectrum, the agency models a world that assumes that disruptions to shipping lanes in the Middle East would persist, leading countries to decide that the risks, and the costs, of importing fossil fuels is too great. Nations might then create more ambitious energy policies, like encouraging greater sales of electric vehicles or faster deployment of nuclear energy.

In such a scenario, global oil demand could plummet by 4.4 million barrels per day, the I.E.A. found. The world currently uses an average of 102.3 million barrels per day.

An aggressive increase in the adoption of electric vehicles alone could displace more than 11 million barrels of oil per day by 2035.

The outlook also forecasts what might happen if countries do not enact new energy policies — and if safe navigation of oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz are restored by the end of 2027.

Under those conditions, oil and gas demand would continue to rise steadily through 2050. The rise in sales of electric vehicles and the decline in costs of solar panels and battery storage would be countered by more fossil fuel use in heavy freight trucks, aviation and petrochemicals.

The result: Carbon dioxide emissions would remain elevated, leading to a 2.9 degree Celsius rise in global temperatures by the end of the century. Scientists have warned that with every fraction of a degree of warming, the risks from deadly heat waves, wildfires, droughts and storms increase significantly.

The Trump administration had publicly pressured the I.E.A. to include the more conservative scenario. Chris Wright, the energy secretary, complained that an agency forecast suggesting that global demand for oil and gas could peak by the end of the decade was “nonsensical.”

The new report argued that “whatever path the world takes,” higher incomes and growing populations are set to increase energy demand. And rising global temperatures will add pressure on energy systems.

For the first time in history, for example, energy needed to keep buildings cool is overtaking energy needed for heating, the I.E.A. said.

The economic impact of the war has been incredibly costly for nations that import fossil fuels and lucrative for exporters: Oil and gas exporters are set to receive an additional $700 billion in sales this year over and above the 10-year average, the I.E.A. said.

The use of coal, the dirtiest fossil fuel, received what the report called a “short term boost” from the Iran war. But in all of the agency’s scenarios, coal use will decline by 2030. That’s in large part because of China, which accounts for more than half of global coal demand but is quickly switching to wind, solar and nuclear energy.

Nuclear power could be another winner. About 90 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity is under construction, the highest level for more than 35 years, the I.E.A. said. More than 50 countries have plans or targets for nuclear power, including new technologies such as small modular reactors.

Diplomats at COP31 said they hoped the report would help encourage efforts to ensure that the world electrifies even faster.

“There will inevitably be short-term pressures,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the co-president of COP31.

He argued that countries must accelerate the transition to more diversified and lower-emissions sources of energy to reduce their exposure to another worldwide energy shortage.

“The answer to a global fossil fuel crisis is not greater long-term dependence on an energy source vulnerable to conflicts overseas,” Mr. Bowen said.
