item.title: Netanyahu Associates Acknowledge Role in Setting Off Election Day Arrests
item.description:
After Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies failed to win an outright majority in last month’s Israeli election, he insisted the vote was stolen, arguing that record turnout by Arab voters was part of a conspiracy to rig the result.

As evidence for his claims, Mr. Netanyahu seized on the arrests of three activists for Raam, an Arab-led opposition party, on the morning of Election Day. The Israeli police said at the time that the men were believed to have been planning to bribe voters, adding that officers had seized envelopes of cash that might have been part of a plot.

Raam denied the allegations, and the activists were ultimately released without charge. But what Mr. Netanyahu did not say at the time was that his own chief of staff and a former aide had been involved in the initial outreach to the police that led to the arrests.

Both aides acknowledged their involvement this week. The suggestion that Mr. Netanyahu’s office had a hand in the arrests of his political opponents has prompted calls for an investigation. The Israeli attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, said on Tuesday that she and the state prosecutor were looking into the matter.

Ram Ben Barak, a centrist lawmaker from the opposition Together party and a former deputy chief of the Mossad intelligence agency, said that the allegations evoked repressive states such as President Vladimir V. Putin’s Russia, in which the police are weaponized as a political tool.

“I would never have imagined that this kind of story would emerge from the Israeli prime minister’s office,” Mr. Ben Barak added.

Mr. Netanyahu’s aides initially denied reports, including in The New York Times, that the police who arrested the three Raam activists on Oct. 27 were acting on a telephone tip provided by the prime minister’s chief of staff, Ido Norden. But on Sunday, after an investigative report by the Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 unearthed new details about the episode, Mr. Netanyahu’s office changed course.

“Criminal information reached Ido Norden, the chief of staff,” his office said in a statement. “He carried out his duty, like any other citizen.”

After an election that left neither Mr. Netanyahu nor the opposition with a clear path to forming a government, critics of the prime minister say the episode shows how far he will go to maintain his grip on power. They also say it reinforces fears that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies have bent Israel’s security agencies to serve their personal agendas, which the prime minister has denied.

The Israeli prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for further comment, nor did the Israeli police or the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency.

On the morning that Israelis headed to the polls, Mr. Netanyahu trumpeted news of the arrests in bluntly racial terms, appealing to right-wing Jewish Israelis to vote because more Arabs were voting than Jews.

“This is an emergency appeal,” he said. “They are trying to steal the elections from us.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party secured more seats in Israel’s Parliament, the Knesset, than any other, even though the opposition parties collectively have a majority.

Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the opposition Yashar party and is Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, has demanded a criminal investigation into the arrests. He has accused Mr. Netanyahu of potentially “planting evidence and deploying the police against Arab citizens of Israel without valid search or arrest warrants.”

The surge in turnout among Arab voters handed the Arab-led parties a historic 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset. After the vote, Mr. Netanyahu initiated an aggressive push to delegitimize the results, at times echoing President Trump’s “stop the steal” campaign after the 2020 U.S. elections.

Israeli election officials have repeatedly said there is no proof of widespread fraud that could affect the results. That has not deterred Likud, which continues to assert that the election was tainted, warning in a statement that the Arab parties would bring about “the Islamification of Israel.”

Raam, the party of the three arrested activists, is a pragmatic Arab-led grouping with Islamist roots. It is one of the two main Arab parties in Israel. Portraying Raam as being linked with possible criminality has some benefit for Mr. Netanyahu as it could complicate any effort by Mr. Eisenkot to form a coalition that relied on the Arab party’s support.

The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency, is separately investigating potential foreign funding in the election — an inquiry that Likud has also invoked to assert that the vote was flawed. But the investigation has not found any widespread bribery or tampering with the election results, Noam Sohlberg, a conservative judge who chairs the Central Elections Committee, said on Tuesday.

Now, after the revelations about the initial contact with the police, Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals say that the real meddling on Election Day may have been perpetrated by the prime minister’s associates.

On Monday, Israel’s national broadcaster, Kan, named the tipster as Daniel Greenberg, who worked in Mr. Netanyahu’s office from 2023 until a few months ago. In a government document, reviewed by The Times, Mr. Greenberg is described as an “adviser on Arab affairs.”

A lawyer for Mr. Greenberg, Avichai Yehosef, confirmed in an interview that his client was the source of the tip, but denied that he had tried to improperly influence the election, saying that Mr. Greenberg had merely passed along information about the activists’ intention to bribe voters.

Mr. Yehosef said that Mr. Greenberg had learned the names of the three Raam activists from an Arab lawmaker. He declined to name the lawmaker.

The three Raam activists were arrested before dawn on Election Day, Oct. 27, at their homes in southern Israel, court filings show. At least two of their homes were searched without warrants, the police later admitted in court.

One of the activists, Dr. Sayyaf Abu Riash, 38, said in an interview that he woke up at roughly 4:30 a.m. that day when the police demanded to enter and search his home. Officers refused to say what they were looking for, Dr. Abu Riash said, before telling him to accompany them to a police station, where he was interrogated him about his involvement in the party.

Dr. Abu Riash said that he campaigned on behalf of Raam but did not hold a formal role. He said Israeli leaders should look favorably on Arab citizens turning out in such high numbers.

“It shows that they feel like they’re part of the country,” he said.

Instead, he said that his arrest had been “used to inspire fear” about the prospect of Arab citizens exercising their democratic rights.

Judge Merav Amar Cohen, who ordered Dr. Abu Riash’s release, criticized the police, saying officers had lacked an evidentiary basis to hold him.

“The investigation files show that the defendant is involved in advocating for the Raam party and even involved in house meetings with candidates,” she wrote in a judgment ordering his release. “But that’s not a crime.”

item.title: After Train Crash, Spain Asks if High-Speed Rail Grew Too Fast
item.description:
Spain is in the middle of a growth spurt. Immigrants are driving the population to a record high of nearly 50 million. Tourism has skyrocketed and is set to attract nearly 100 million people, 25 million more than in 2016. With one of Europe’s fastest-growing economies, Spain has invested tens of billions of euros in digitalization and renewable energy.

But a horrific train crash that killed 69 people last month, only nine months after a collision on the same high-speed line killed scores more, has raised concerns about the state of Spanish civil infrastructure. It has also left Spaniards asking if their country has grown too fast for its own good.

With national elections set for this month, infrastructure has moved from esoteric policy papers to the campaign trail.

Opposition politicians say the left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has let the country go to seed. Some experts argue that his government was overly focused on new investments instead of maintaining old ones like roads, water systems and the high-speed rail network, the world’s second-largest, behind China’s. One think tank found that spending per high-speed rail passenger fell by more than a quarter in the decade leading to 2024.

“The system is under strain,” said Pere Navarro, the Spanish civil servant responsible for highway traffic. Spain’s infrastructure and public services, he said, were designed for “when there were 40 million of us” but now “we have a population of 50 million and welcome 100 million tourists every year.”

Mr. Sánchez’ government said that, though Spain needed to increase investment in its railways, it was the center-right former government that led the country until eight years ago that had eroded infrastructure, and especially railway infrastructure, with years of austerity policies.

Mr. Sánchez, pressed on the lack of maintenance in a television interview on Wednesday, argued that his government had worked to “reverse the cuts to the railway system” by his conservative predecessor. He also promised the equivalent of an additional $21 billion on maintenance and safety spending through 2030.

Much of Spain’s infrastructure dates to a previous boom era, soon after the country joined a precursor to the European Union in 1986. Suddenly awash in the bloc’s funds, it spent the 1990s revamping its industrial capitals, like Barcelona and Bilbao, and building a sprawling high-speed rail system and broader highways.

By the early 2000s, as Spain kept spending billions on transit infrastructure, it gained global renown for its high-capacity rails and roads. But a series of setbacks hit the country hard. Investment in infrastructure fell off after the financial crisis in 2008 and the popping of Spain’s housing bubble.

As Spain became wealthier and E.U. priorities shifted east, European funds dried up. Then, after the 2008 financial crash, Europe’s sovereign debt crisis nearly halved public investment in Spain, once higher than the European average. The spending didn’t recover under either right- or left-leaning governments. Now, Spain is spending, in real terms, about 25 percent less on infrastructure than it did in 2000, according to the Valencian Institute of Economic Research.

In 2018, Mr. Sánchez, of the Socialist Party, took office. After managing Spain through the coronavirus pandemic, he used a round of enormous E.U. recovery funds to focus on growth.

“Spain is in fashion,” Mr. Sanchez said at a tourism fair last year.

In a sign of his confidence in Spanish rail infrastructure, his government proposed banning short flights to cut carbon emissions. He used increased tax revenues from an influx of immigrant workers to fill the government coffers and offer popular subsidies and social benefits.

As the country’s gross domestic product soared, its investment in infrastructure didn’t keep pace. Last year, a national blackout exposed the weaknesses of the country’s saturated energy grid. It depends increasingly on the renewable sources that Mr. Sánchez’ government has prioritized, a factor that experts have said may have made it less stable. Analysts and energy companies also say the grid’s limitations make it harder to supply electricity to new construction projects, slowing building projects and contributing to a housing shortage. Protests over housing and high rents this year prompted Mr. Sánchez to call for early elections.

The blackout inspired a book by the economic think tank Funcas that argued that “political considerations influencing decisions” contributed to obsolescence and breakdowns of Spain’s transport infrastructure, water networks and energy assets. The authors said that the government should instead “prioritize maintaining existing infrastructure over new investment.”

They weren’t alone.

“In Spain, many things that once worked well now work poorly,” Ramón González Férriz, a political analyst, wrote in a much-discussed article in El Confidencial, a center-right news outlet, after the recent train crash. He blamed the government for prioritizing benefits and subsidies over maintaining public works that, he wrote, “take a long time to bear fruit and may go unnoticed by voters.”

The government’s initial response to the crash was not to focus on maintenance flaws but to blame the human error — revealed in leaked audio from a train traffic control center — in which a controller directed one high-speed train into a stalled train on the same track. But the second deadly crash in a year prompted inevitable questions about railway infrastructure and safety.

The transportation minister, Óscar Puente, who subsequently resigned, lamented that because the government did not control a majority of lawmakers in Parliament, it could not pass a budget that invested more in railway maintenance. Since then, Mr. Sánchez has responded to criticism with a mix of blame for conservative predecessors, defense of his government’s spending level and promises to increase it.

Conservative opponents, including from the Popular Party, which leads election polls, say Mr. Sánchez has full responsibility for any infrastructure shortcomings after eight years in power.

Spain is suffering from “continued negligence” under Mr. Sánchez that has put Spaniards at risk, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the Popular Party leader, said this month.

Train usage in Spain has risen drastically since 2021, when Mr. Sánchez’ government opened the country’s market for high-speed passenger trains to competitors. Ticket prices fell by more than 40 percent, and hundreds of miles of new high-speed rail routes were opened. Last year, 44.5 million passengers used high-speed rail, twice as many as in 2019.

But according to the Institute of Economic Studies, a Madrid think tank associated with Spain’s largest association of employers, maintenance spending per high-speed passenger dropped 27.5 percent between 2015 and 2024. At the time of the accident, Spain was among the European countries that spent the least on maintaining its rail network.

Spain’s passengers had begun to notice delays, with on-time arrivals dropping nearly 10 points to roughly 86 percent in 2024, according to Spain’s competition regulator.

Train drivers warned last year of track deterioration on the high-speed route to Seville, the line where the crashes occurred.

Beyond the issue of high-speed rail maintenance, transportation experts have said that Spain’s entire strategy of prioritizing high-speed rail makes little sense because over 80 percent of Spain’s passenger rail trips last year were on shorter-distance commuter lines that have suffered from years of neglect.

Spain’s Independent Authority for Fiscal Responsibility, an autonomous state-appointed body, reported that between 1990 and 2018, Spain invested 15 times more on high-speed rail than on commuter rail, a trend that continued under Mr. Sánchez.

But Mr. Sánchez’ focus on high-speed rail was not just a government priority. Mr. Puente, the former transportation minister, pointed out at the time that regional politicians all over the country had demanded high-speed rail, regardless of their political affiliation.

“Look at this country’s history over the past 20 or 30 years,” he said. “If you don’t have high-speed rail, you’re nobody.”

item.title: First ‘Family Photo’ With Putin Since Ukraine Invasion Raises Awkward Questions for Some Leaders
item.description:
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, President Vladimir Putin of Russia has avoided most international summits and, as a result, has been absent from the staid and stage-managed “family photo” leaders pose for at the gatherings.

On Thursday, not only was he back in the frame at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, but he was front and center, standing next to China’s leader, Xi Jinping, the host. President Trump stood on the other side of Mr. Xi.

Mr. Putin’s prominent turn on the world stage alongside a number of leaders who have spent years condemning him and trying to isolate him over his war in Ukraine drew criticism in some of their home countries. The image prompted questions about the message it sends about the international resolve to counter Russian aggression.

In the days leading up to the summit, speculation had built over whether any leaders would boycott the photo, after several foreign ministers attending a Group of 20 meeting last month in Atlanta refused to be photographed alongside Russia’s top diplomat, Sergey Lavrov. In the end, that photo opportunity was scrapped altogether.

On Wednesday night, Mr. Putin appeared alongside those leaders for a photo at the summit banquet. On Thursday, the leaders posed once more as the first agenda item of the day.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia, responding to repeated questions from reporters, said it was a matter of “good manners” to accommodate the wishes of the host nation, China, adding that his country’s stance on the war remained firm.

“China is our host here. I respect that,” he said on Wednesday. “But we’ll also make our position very clear when it comes to Ukraine.”

The Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organizations had urged Mr. Albanese to sit out the photo, saying it would “normalize” Mr. Putin and his conduct.

Before the photo, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada was asked whether he would participate and how he would “publicly demonstrate” the repudiation of Mr. Putin that Canadians expect from their leader.

“The short answer on the protocol of participating in the photo, yes, I will participate in the photo, out of respect for the host,” Mr. Carney said, adding that Canada’s reproach of Russia’s actions was apparent in its policies.

item.title: Villa Where Trump, Xi and Putin Will Meet Once Hosted Kim Jong-il
item.description:
The first-ever meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will be held in Kylin Villa, a secluded lakeside resort that has also hosted the North Korean dictator Kim Jong-il, envoys for the Dalai Lama and Xi Jinping’s father.

It was also the setting for a surreal dinner in 2016 for four detained Hong Kong booksellers, part of an effort to convince them to cooperate with the Chinese authorities.

On Thursday, President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir V. Putin were expected to discuss nuclear arms, the war in Iran and other issues at the luxury guesthouse surrounded by the forest of the Qilin Mountain in northwestern Shenzhen.

The resort was originally built to house hundreds of Chinese officials traveling to nearby Hong Kong for the 1997 handover to China, which ended more than 150 years of British rule over the city. At the time, Hong Kong did not have the capacity to host all the officials from Beijing as well as local governments that would likely stop in Shenzhen on their way to Hong Kong, potentially holding key events and meetings, according to a 2020 memoir by Li Zibin, who was mayor of Shenzhen at the time.

“This was an event of global significance and a momentous occasion for China,” he wrote. “Yet the city’s existing reception facilities were far from sufficient to meet the anticipated demand.”

As a result, Shenzhen built the sprawling Kylin or Qilin complex, named after a mythical Chinese beast that is considered an omen for prosperity. It covers more than 200 acres with banquet halls, a golf course and villas designed to look European.

North Korea’s former leader Kim Jong-il stayed at Kylin Villa when he made an unannounced trip to China in January 2006 and visited the special economic zone of Shenzhen, prompting speculation that he would open his country’s economy to private enterprise.

In 2002, Mr. Xi’s father, Xi Zhongxun, a former senior Chinese Communist Party leader who was living in Shenzhen at the time, spent time resting there after he was diagnosed with cancer, a few months before he died.

It was also the site of negotiations between the Chinese and envoys for the Dalai Lama in 2008, two months after a demonstration in Lhasa, Tibet’s capital, turned violent.

Among the resort’s more unusual guests was Lam Wing-kee, a bookseller in Hong Kong who was abducted and imprisoned for selling tomes banned in mainland China. Mr. Lam was taken to Kylin in 2016, after more than four months of detention.

Waiting for him there were three of his associates, staff at a Hong Kong publishing house that also dealt in banned books. They were served dinner in the company of a guard and were monitored by three security cameras. One of the men urged Mr. Lam and the other associates to cooperate with the authorities and handed them each about $15,300.

When the three leaders visit the villa on Thursday, it may be a little less luxurious than it has been in the past. A finance report for the complex posted on the Shenzhen government’s website said that its budget had been reduced by 19 percent compared to last year. The main reason, the report said, was to follow Beijing’s calls for local governments to optimize their spending and “get used to tightening our belts.”

Pei-Lin Wu contributed to this report.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
The International Court of Justice is issuing its ruling Thursday morning on whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a landmark decision years in the making that will have far-reaching implications.

If found guilty, Myanmar would be the first state — as opposed to an individual — held to account for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. Judge Iwasawa Yuji, the president of the I.C.J., began reading out its ruling in the morning. It could take hours to complete.

The African nation of Gambia brought the case against Myanmar to the court, the United Nations’ top judicial body located in The Hague, Netherlands, in 2019. Since then, 11 other countries have formally lent their support to the case. The United States has already deemed the Myanmar security forces’ campaign of violence against the Rohingya, which culminated in a frenzy of killing, sexual violence and mass arson nine years ago, to be a genocide.

A guilty verdict against Myanmar could have bearing on another genocide case at the I.C.J.: South Africa’s claim against Israel for the violence in Gaza.

The case hinges on whether Myanmar acted with the specific intent to physically destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group. Under the U.N. definition, committing acts of cultural destruction is not enough for such violence to be considered genocide. There must also be proven intent — a hard factor to determine.

The genocide case was prompted by “clearance operations” in Myanmar in 2017, when the country’s security forces and ethnic Rakhine mobs rampaged through Rohingya communities, burning about 400 villages and killing at least 10,000 people, according to U.N. estimates. The operation was collective punishment in response to attacks by Rohingya militants on police posts and a military base.

The massacres against the Rohingya led to the most rapid exodus of refugees in recent history, and about 1.2 million Rohingya now live in crowded refugee camps in Bangladesh.

A finding that Myanmar committed genocide could set an important legal precedent and pave the way for determining reparations for Rohingya survivors. It could also order Myanmar to halt continuing violence against the Rohingya. The court, however, does not have the power to enforce its rulings and may depend on support from the United Nations Security Council, which has two members — China and Russia — that would most likely protect Myanmar.

Here is what else to know.

What is the International Court of Justice? The court, also known as the World Court, was established by the United Nations Charter in 1945 to settle legal disputes between its member states. It typically consists of 15 judges, elected by the U.N. General Assembly and Security Council.

item.title: Half a world from The Hague, Rohingya refugees know nothing of a genocide trial.
item.description:
In the refugee camps of Bangladesh, I kept asking: What did the Rohingya, who were violently expelled from Myanmar nearly a decade ago, think about the genocide trial at the International Court of Justice in The Hague? Did they expect the ruling on Thursday to go their way and hold Myanmar accountable for committing genocide?

Mostly, the answer was that they didn’t think about it because they didn’t know about it.

Many of the Rohingya people who fled Myanmar in 2016 and 2017, the years covered in the genocide trial, endured atrocities firsthand. After Rohingya militants attacked police posts and an army base nine years ago, Myanmar security forces responded swiftly with what they called “clearance operations.” They killed, they raped and they burned some 400 villages. Nearly all Rohingya life in Myanmar’s far western Rakhine State was wiped out.

In 2017, I watched Rohingya pour into Bangladesh, bedraggled and traumatized. Most had been on the run for days, through mud and monsoon downpours. They had left behind family members who were shot dead, some of them beheaded.

But for such ethnic cleansing to be legally deemed genocide, the perpetrators’ intent must also be proved. The Rohingya understand that the bloodletting that prompted Gambia to lodge its case at the court in 2019 was rooted in decades of persecution.

In the 1980s, a citizenship law rendered Rohingya effectively stateless. By the 2000s, Myanmar’s authorities had imposed apartheid conditions. Rohingya had to pay extortionate fees for basic paperwork, like marriage licenses or birth certificates, if they could obtain them at all. They could not travel freely. Rohingya women were warned not to bear more than a couple of children. Many mosques were shuttered. Schooling was often off-limits.

Thousands of Rohingya were also forced into internment camps in Myanmar, where coils of barbed wire separated them from the rest of the country.

Despite enduring these deprivations and more, most of the people I asked in the refugee camps had little way of knowing what was happening half a world away at a court in The Hague.

Shomina Ara’s husband was killed in a mortar attack on their home. She still has shrapnel from the strike embedded in her body. Her daughter has a chunk of metal lodged in her foot.

“I don’t really understand this word ‘genocide,’” Ms. Ara said. “I know that people in Myanmar want all the Rohingya to disappear forever.”

item.title: Aung San Suu Kyi did not condemn the pogroms against the Rohingya.
item.description:
During one of the first hearings of the case, in 2019, a Nobel laureate defended the state of Myanmar against the accusation of genocide at the International Court of Justice.

It was Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, then Myanmar’s de facto civilian leader, who had been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 for her nonviolent resistance to her country’s military government.

But her image was tarnished during her years at the helm when she and her government refused to directly criticize the frenzy of killing, rape and mass arson committed against the Rohingya by Myanmar security forces in 2016 and 2017.

Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi’s office called a well documented campaign of sexual violence against the Rohingya “fake rape.” When questioned directly, she denied that the Rohingya had endured ethnic cleansing. She described extensive testimony about the atrocities as “a huge iceberg of misinformation.” She even avoided using the word “Rohingya,” helping to buttress the military’s false claim that the Muslim ethnicity did not exist and was instead a collection of illegal immigrants from neighboring Bangladesh.

As leader, Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi, whose father was the founder of the nation’s army and is regarded as an independence hero, did not have complete authority over the country and was bound by a power-sharing agreement with the military. Her supporters have said that she had no choice but to try to placate the generals with her personal defense of them. They say that her eventual ouster in 2021 — she is now 81 and still under detention — proved how little power she really had to counter their racism and violence against the Rohingya.

item.title: COP31 Climate Talks Are Bigger Than Ever, but Few Are There to Negotiate
item.description:
There’s a paradox at the center of this year’s United Nations climate conference.

The event is bigger than ever, as tens of thousands of lanyard-wearing participants stream in every morning, grab free apples and chocolate at the entrance, and then proceed to pack every corridor of a gargantuan expo center.

But the end result is expected to be modest, if not marginal.

George Hussey, an Irish attendee, surveyed the crowds this week amid the echo of competing climate panels, and posed what has become a common question.

“What is all this for?” he asked.

Decades ago, the work to address climate change consisted of smallish, technical affairs. But the conferences have boomed into both trade shows and networking events, offering chances to lobby, brainstorm and even commiserate.

This year’s 12-day conference, known as COP31 and held in Antalya, Turkey, seemingly marks the completion of this transformation. Only about 20 percent of the record 92,000 registered participants are there for the formal negotiations.

Many attendees wonder whether the crowds are excessive or whether they prove climate change’s salience even as it appeared to have slipped as a priority in a world focused on conflicts, A.I. and economic problems. Either way, an event often judged for a single formal outcome now consists of thousands of outcomes, as specific as the people in attendance.

“Everybody has their own piece of the puzzle here that they’re interested in,” said Mr. Hussey, a member of Ireland’s Climate Change Advisory Council.

The participants this year include environmental insurance experts, American law students, advocates for sustainable aviation fuels, and one man wearing a Santa hat saying SustainaClaus. Some came for an “Olympics” on building energy savings.

Daniel Cusworth, an American scientist at Carbon Mapper, pitched tools to governments that could uncover large sources of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Carlos Garcia, a Mexican filmmaker, screened a short documentary on landfills, rendered vividly enough to see the flies through 3-D glasses. Bashiir Mohamed, the leader of a Somali green energy association, came to rally funding so that 100,000 homes could obtain solar panels, and with it the chance to power phones, refrigerators and air-conditioning units.

“Energy changes everything,” Mr. Mohamed said.

There’s been plenty of sentiment that the annual climate conference has grown beyond its purpose. The event’s carbon footprint has increased 25-fold over three decades. Two years ago, 22 environmental leaders and scientists wrote a letter to the United Nations calling for streamlining the event with “smaller, more frequent, solution-driven meetings.”

But Johan Rockström, a Swedish scientist who signed the letter, says he has had second thoughts. The big gatherings “manifest to the world that this is something to take seriously,” he said. And they have meaning to the participants, too. For almost two weeks, people work long hours in what can feel like “planetary-scale therapy sessions.”

His only reservation: that the good feeling might be unearned.

“We are still able to tell ourselves that we have done everything we can,” said Dr. Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. “Is this a way for the climate community to feel less frustrated?”

Advocates for the U.N. process note that it has made some key progress. Global temperatures had once been projected to rise almost 4 degrees Celsius (7.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels. With nations’ commitments under the Paris climate agreement in 2015, plus the spread of renewable energy, warming is now on track for 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) if current policies continue.

Over the years, COP organizers have set up — and enlarged — an agenda outside of the formal negotiations for voluntary measures from nations, cities, businesses and investors.

Whereas formal negotiations used to be the centerpiece, now “it’s just a little dot in the middle,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of Climate Analytics, a climate science and policy institute based in Berlin.

This year, for instance, negotiators are again fighting over references to fossil fuels in a final agreement, with oil-producing countries capable of blocking any deal in the consensus-based process. But on the sidelines, there have been dozens of events devoted to transitioning away from coal, oil and gas, and a handful of nations announced new domestic pledges.

Those hints of momentum, plus being around like-minded people, “makes COP really fulfilling, even if on a bigger level it’s a pretty dire situation we’re facing,” said Natalie Jones, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, an independent research organization.

There are a handful of reasons this year’s COP grew so large. Turkey is a convenient destination from Europe, Asia and Africa. Antalya, the host city, has an ample supply of hotel rooms. And Turkey has padded the list with 14,000 guests — civil servants, academics and politicians. COP31 is more than twice the size of last year’s event, held in a Brazilian city on the edge of the rainforest, where organizers used cruise ships to ease hotel room shortages.

It helps that this year’s climate talks have taken place under near-ideal conditions, at least after Turkey fixed transportation chaos that plagued the first days.

Every day, the temperatures have risen to almost exactly 70 degrees. The expo, for all its scale, has plenty of charming touches: work stands where locals draw calligraphy and whittle wooden spinning tops and a domed food court where speakers play fake birdsong. An ornamental water channel cuts through the event halls, zigzagging around coffee shops. (One participant, inevitably, fell in.)

“The venue is great,” said Gerald Miles, an Australian conservationist and longtime COP attendee who was fine-tuning a speech near a pagoda. Among the highlights? “The apples and chocolate,” he said.

Mr. Hussey, of Ireland, said he has concluded that attending COP was a bit like “being back in school.” Everywhere he looked, there was something to learn. As he spoke, one of Ireland’s former presidents walked by. Then its climate and energy minister.

“Unfortunately, no matter how long you stay here, you can only tap a little,” Mr. Hussey said. “You wouldn’t want to live your life in this weird place. It’s not natural. But a little bit every year. You realize, we’re not on our own here.”

item.title: A village was burned, its people killed or exiled. Was it part of a genocide?
item.description:
As his village burned, Mustafa Kamal somehow kept his family safe.

Husband and wife, three sons, three daughters, a granddaughter, they ran until their breath ran out. They stumbled past bodies of people they knew, shot by Myanmar’s security forces. They slogged through mud that claimed some of their clothes and trekked over jungle passes thick with leeches. Days later, when they finally crossed a river into Bangladesh, they rowed past swollen bodies of other Rohingya Muslims who never made it to the other side alive.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice in The Hague is ruling whether the atrocities against the Rohingya ethnic minority constitute a genocide waged by the Myanmar state. The killing, gang rape and mass arson reached a furious zenith in 2017, building on years of systematic persecution. Three quarters of a million Rohingya flooded into Bangladesh in a matter of weeks, the most rapid refugee exodus in recent history. And more kept coming.

A judgment in a country half a world away would matter, Mr. Kamal told me. It would acknowledge the fate of his home, Zammona, one of 400 Rohingya villages that were obliterated by Myanmar security forces nine years ago.

But sitting in the dark, cramped shelter that is now his home in Bangladesh, part of what is now the world’s largest refugee settlement, Mr. Kamal said that the trauma did not end nine years ago. For the Rohingya, he said, misery never ends.

item.title: On nukes, Trump says, ‘It’s very hard to give them up.’ It’s been done before.
item.description:
President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia were vague in their opening statements about the nature of the conversation they were about to enter, mostly repeating platitudes about strengthening security and stability.

President Trump, by contrast, was a bit more specific. He described four topics he planned to raise: reducing nuclear arsenals of the three nations represented at the table, cracking down on nuclear proliferation to smaller powers — his justification for the U.S. attack on Iran — resolving the war in Ukraine and restraining the excesses of the International Criminal Court.

“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Mr. Trump said, reading from prepared remarks. But he noted that “it’s very hard to give them up as a leader of a country.”

Perhaps, but his predecessors have done it. One doesn’t have to go back too far in American diplomatic history to recall how it was accomplished in a series of arms control treaties. In the 1960s, the United States had more than 30,000 warheads. In the mid-1980s, the Soviets had about 40,000. Today, each has slightly more than 5,000, and only 1,550 deployed under the New Start Treaty that expired this year.

That is a huge reduction in raw numbers. For a while after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the United States was paying billions of dollars to Russia in return for dismantling thousands of its warheads, blending down their nuclear cores and using them to power nuclear plants across the United States.

But that program, once the crown jewel of cooperation between Washington and Moscow in the post-Cold War world, has long since expired. And now both countries have been reluctant to drop their nuclear inventories much below existing levels.

In his opening remarks, Mr. Trump never discussed the real sticking point: China, which was never a party to previous nuclear reduction treaties, is now intent on building up to at least current Russian and U.S. levels. And Mr. Trump has not discussed ways to deter Beijing from moving ahead with that plan or even providing the world with any discussion of its intentions.

At the summit, Mr. Xi, for his part, mentioned a utopian goal that has essentially fallen off the agenda of superpowers: eliminating all nuclear weapons from the earth. (President Barack Obama set a similar goal, while acknowledging that it would probably not happen in his lifetime.) Mr. Xi did not discuss the fact that China has the fastest-growing arsenal on earth.

Mr. Trump seems unlikely to agree to reduce the U.S. arsenal to Chinese levels. During the Obama administration, even the idea of dropping below 1,000 strategic weapons — those that can cross oceans — generated objections from the Pentagon, where officials feared that in a nuclear exchange it would be impossible to guarantee there would be enough survivable American weapons for a so-called second strike.

Nor does Mr. Putin have much of an incentive. With the Russian economy suffering, especially in an era of sanctions on oil sales, his nuclear weapons are one of the key sources of Russian power.

The Chinese have little interest in a two-tiered system in which they live with a smaller deterrent than Washington’s or Moscow’s. That minimum deterrent was Mao Zedong’s strategy for decades — but Mr. Xi has made clear that as a rising superpower, China will be a peer of its existing adversaries, with an arsenal to match.

item.title: China Bars Bloomberg Reporter From Trilateral Talks for Asking a Question
item.description:
Seated at a long table across from the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, President Trump had just finished thanking his host when a reporter called out a question: Had Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia, been disloyal to the United States?

The president did not answer. Mr. Xi looked toward the gaggle of reporters and then away as a security guard moved in and blocked a camera that had been recording the exchange.

Chinese officials later barred the journalist, Annmarie Hordern, a Bloomberg TV reporter, from covering Mr. Xi’s next major event, perhaps the most important of the day in Shenzhen: a trilateral meeting of the leaders of the United States, China and Russia.

It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.

When Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia met in the first-ever summit of the leaders of those three countries, the reporter was prevented from entering the room.

A White House official said that the U.S. side had tried to reinstate the journalist but that Chinese officials refused, according to a report shared among television journalists. Reporters at the summit were told that it was extremely rude to shout a question. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to emailed questions about the reporter’s exclusion. A spokeswoman for Bloomberg News declined to comment.

In the United States, it is routine for the president to answer impromptu questions from the press corps. Over the past week, Mr. Trump has spoken about Mr. Huang several times. Mr. Huang is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy. (China has denied the espionage claims.)

When China hosts official events, it tightly controls the access of reporters, often allowing only state media outlets into major events or giving foreign journalists selective access. Over the years, China has expelled many foreign reporters, including most recently a New York Times correspondent. Chinese officials also try to influence international outlets by threatening to not grant them the accreditation that their reporters need to work in the country.

Looking out and seeing a lack of the usual fleet of American photographers and recognizable reporters who track his every move, Mr. Trump seemed to gently criticize the restrictions. In his remarks to Mr. Xi, the president praised the organization of the summit. “It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed,” he told the Chinese leader.

Mr. Xi, whose comments reach the Chinese public via speeches and remarks carried in state media outlets and rarely has unfiltered moments, does not hold news conferences or directly engage with reporters.

Previous American leaders have used state visits to China to push Beijing to be more open with the news media. During a joint news conference that U.S. officials forcefully negotiated during President Barack Obama’s trip to Beijing in 2014, Mr. Xi took a question from an American reporter about how the Chinese leader viewed Washington’s renewed focus on Asia. When Mr. Xi visited Washington in 2015, he took another question on cybersecurity from an American reporter.

Mr. Trump broke with that tradition when he traveled to China in 2017 and refused to take questions. When he visited again in May, he answered some questions from journalists but did not hold a formal news conference with Mr. Xi. During his trip to Shenzhen this week, the leaders again did not hold a joint press conference.

Peter Baker contributed reporting from Shenzhen, China.

item.title: Some leaders flew private to the APEC summit in Manila, but not Mexico’s president.
item.description:
Many of the world leaders who arrived in the Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum traveled on private or presidential planes. President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico opted for a more low-key approach.

Ms. Sheinbaum arrived in Shenzhen by commercial flight, a grueling journey. On Saturday, she posted a video from Mexico City International Airport saying she would first fly to Tijuana and then on to Shenzhen. The three-hour domestic leg was followed by a flight to Shenzhen lasting roughly 15 hours.

The video showed her sitting in the terminal, greeting travelers and taking photos with fans at the boarding gate.

“It’s practically a two-day flight, and on top of that, there’s the time change,” she told EFE, the Spanish news agency.

After touching down in Shenzhen on Monday, Ms. Sheinbaum took a shuttle bus to a red carpet on the tarmac, where she was greeted by Chinese officials and dancers.

Chinese social media users praised Ms. Sheinbaum’s modest mode of travel as pragmatic. On Weibo, China’s version of X, posts about her arrival drew more than 10 million views.

It is not the first time Ms. Sheinbaum has flown commercial as president. She did the same for other major diplomatic trips — including the Group of 20 summit in Brazil in 2024 and the Group of 7 summit in Canada last year.

When she flew to Brazil commercially in 2024, her government said in a statement that it was in accordance with one of the principles of her government, which was austerity.

The practice of Mexican presidents traveling commercially began in December 2018 under Ms. Sheinbaum’s predecessor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who refused to board Mexico’s presidential jet upon taking office and left it parked for more than four years before selling it in 2023. He described the plane as an “insult to the people” and an example of excess, and vowed to forgo the luxuries often seen as political perks. He also said he would cut his salary, convert the sprawling presidential residence into an arts and culture center and dissolved the 8,000-member military presidential guard.

The Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner was ordered by former President Felipe Calderón and used by his successor, Enrique Peña Nieto. Mr. López Obrador spent several years struggling to find a buyer before selling the aircraft to Tajikistan for $92 million.

Jiawei Wang contributed reporting.

item.title: Putin Joins Trump and Xi in Condemning Nuclear War as Europe Watches Closely
item.description:
The leaders of China, Russia and the United States agreed in a joint statement after their meeting on Thursday that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

Just two years ago, the Russian leader, President Vladimir V. Putin, expanded his country’s guidelines justifying the use of nuclear weapons, and his arsenal remains the world’s largest. The meeting on Thursday was not expected to produce any change to that policy.

Mr. Putin’s posturing at the summit in Shenzhen, China, held on the sidelines of an Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting, was being watched closely in Europe, where Moscow’s nuclear calculus has been a major concern during Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Rishi Paul, a nuclear deterrence expert at the European Leadership Network, a research group in London, said Mr. Putin “views nuclear weapons as a tool for coercion.”

“It’s a studied ambiguity,” Mr. Paul added. “He is sowing fear by us trying to decipher, ‘What does he mean, exactly?’”

Mr. Paul noted that Russia had recently changed its nuclear doctrine, which guides when nuclear weapons are developed and potentially deployed during war.

That does not mean Russia is looking to rush into nuclear war, Mr. Paul added. Mr. Putin said earlier in the summit that regional leaders had a “joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.”

The statement released after the trilateral meeting on Thursday cited a commitment by China, Russia and the United States to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. Mr. Putin has sought to avoid a nuclear arms race with the United States that could start if Washington builds up its warheads amid concerns about China’s rapidly growing arsenal, said Nicole Grajewski, a nuclear and Russia expert at Sciences Po, a Paris university.

Ms. Grajewski said that Russia’s expanded nuclear policy largely sought to deter European countries in NATO that have supported Ukraine in the nearly five-year war against Moscow.

“The Russians are very good at being duplicitous and multiple things happening at once,” Ms. Grajewski said after the leaders’ meeting on Thursday.

The commitment announced on Thursday to reduce nuclear risk, she said, “seems very empty.”

“I don’t see this turning into a momentum toward rapid reductions or caps on nuclear forces,” Ms. Grajewski added. “It’s really shallow in nature.”

item.title: In a Rohingya Refugee Camp, Jubilation but Also Apprehension
item.description:
It was raining in the Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh on Thursday, unusual for this time of year. One of my strongest memories of reporting on the 2017 exodus from Myanmar was the constant rain, turning jungle paths into muddy treachery.

But the drizzle didn’t stop hundreds of Rohingya men from gathering outdoors in front of a screen at 3 p.m. local time. In prayer caps and their finest clothes, they leaned in close to hear the International Court of Justice, which was issuing its ruling on whether Myanmar had committed genocide, define them as a distinct ethnic group that had suffered the gravest of atrocities: killing, sexual assault, the incineration of their villages.

Few of them spoke English, much less the legalese emanating from The Hague. Nonetheless, they watched.

Salauddin, 70, once a principal of a high school in Maungdaw Township, the site of some of the worst violence unleashed by Myanmar security forces, sat in the front row.

“I know it was genocide myself, and I hope that the court will say that,” he said.

As the legal proceeding dragged on, men left the viewing party at Jamtoli camp for the mosque. The call to prayer echoed. Such daily rites were banned by the Myanmar government in much of Rakhine State, the Rohingya homeland, one of many limits designed to erase the Rohingya identity.

The men wandered back. The judges were still talking. Nearby, vendors sold puffed rice and dried fish. Then the live broadcast cut off, and an announcement in the Rohingya language prematurely delivered the news: The court had recognized that Myanmar had committed a genocide against them. The explosion of cheers rivaled the biggest sporting match. Men wept. Everyone, it seemed, took selfies.

It took two and a half hours until the final verdict was read out.

The jubilation was electric. The announcer thanked everyone: the Bangladeshi government for hosting about 1.2 million Rohingya, 11 countries including the Maldives and Germany for adding their support to the case and, most of all, the African nation of Gambia that brought the genocide case against Myanmar on behalf of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.

This was peak time to be Gambia. Rohingya boys and men gathered in a circle and jumped up and down, chanting in unison a single word: “Gambia.”

I asked one boy where Gambia was. Europe, he answered, though he said he wasn’t exactly sure. Regardless, it was a wonderful country, he said.

The crowds thinned. People walked through muddy alleys, night obscuring puddles, on their way back to their tarpaulin shelters in what is the world’s largest refugee settlement. Mohammed Yeasin Zuhar, 23, cradled his baby boy, only a month-and-a-half old, and said the ruling filled him with joy because his son might not have to grow up in these camps, these vast zones of insecurity.

Here, human traffickers kidnap children, and militants engage in running gun battles. An hour or so before the reading of the judgment began, I heard three gun shots pop nearby.

It was past curfew. I had to leave the camps. A group of Rohingya provided security, their arms spread to form a cordon around me, as a woman, their eyes searching for danger.

But refugees broke through anyway, with tales of woe — a family member killed, a sister raped, a child who didn’t survive the arduous escape from Myanmar. These tragedies continued after 2016 and 2017, the years ruled a genocide by the I.C.J.

I did not know what to say. I understood, like they did, that the court ruling might not change their lives anytime soon. Chances of the Rohingya returning home are slim. The court lacks enforcement powers.

The rain, though, had stopped.

item.title: Major Powers Vow to Increase Oil Supply Amid Global Energy Transition
item.description:
Among the four points the leaders of China, Russia and the United States agreed to on Thursday was a promise to work together to increase the production and supply of “refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

Their resolve is striking for a few reasons.

The wars led by two of them — Russia and the United States — have caused global oil prices to spike, creating a lot of economic pain for oil-importing nations. That has in turn accelerated their transition away from imported fossil fuel energy sources.

Electric vehicle sales have increased in many major markets, except the United States. And the International Energy Agency recently projected in an annual report that the world would add renewable energy capacity, led by solar, far faster over the next five years than it had in recent years because of what it called “unprecedented disruptions to global energy markets since the outbreak of the Iran war.”

“Renewables, already expanding at a record pace before the current energy crisis, are set to see strong growth across a wider range of countries around the world in the coming years as governments seek to strengthen energy security and reduce their exposure to imported fuels and volatile prices,” the agency said.

On Thursday, in its Energy Outlook Report, the agency went further, concluding that the war against Iran had permanently altered the appetite in many countries for imported oil, especially for oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy corridors.

How would the United States, Russia and China would increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products? That remains unclear. All three nations are refining powerhouses. But Russia’s refineries have been damaged in recent months by Ukrainian attacks. A significant amount of Russian crude oil is now being imported and refined in other countries, including China and India.

These three big countries have different agendas for how the world will be powered in the coming years. Russia and the United States are among the world’s biggest oil producers. They want fossil fuels to remain the main energy source of the global economy. China is leading the world to a very different energy future, one that relies on solar, wind, batteries and battery-powered vehicles for energy — all of which China dominates.

It is also striking that Thursday’s joint statement comes during global climate talks, where most countries (except the United States) have been discussing how to slow down global climate change, which is mainly driven by the burning of oil, gas and coal.

item.title: Trump Seeks to Project Power Abroad While Forced to Share It at Home
item.description:
This was the picture President Trump wanted for years: a trio of global titans sitting down together, just the three of them, a 21st-century conclave seemingly shaping the course of world events. At least in his eyes, it projected gravity, it projected grandeur, it projected power.

But the image of Mr. Trump flexing strength with his counterparts at a historic summit in China contrasted sharply with the drastically changing power dynamic for him back home. While he sought to use the meeting with the leaders of China and Russia to signal that he remains a giant on the international stage, Mr. Trump soon will have to share control with ascendant Democrats in Washington.

It says a lot about this president at this point in his rocky tenure that he would rather meet with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia than with Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic congressional leaders who have yet to be invited to the White House since this month’s election. He offered hugs and arm pats and broad smiles to the autocrats, even as his administration has threatened criminal investigations of Democrats who pursue aggressive oversight of his administration next year.

“We are really making history,” Mr. Trump said with a note of pride at the beginning of the trilateral meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin here in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. As leaders of the big powers, he added, the three of them were addressing “issues impacting not just our people but the entire planet.”

He nodded to Mr. Xi. “It’s an honor for me to be with you,” he said. Then to Mr. Putin, he said, “It’s an honor for me to be with you.”

While a gripping photo op, the meeting produced no real breakthroughs, nor did it seem likely to lead to any. None of the traditional diplomatic spadework was done in advance to achieve concrete outcomes. And while the leaders issued a joint statement embracing goals like energy development and reduction of nuclear risks, it was not clear that sustained discussions would follow.

Instead, it was mainly an expression of power, which to Mr. Trump has always been the coin of the realm. Even after voters decisively repudiated him in the midterm elections, he has sought to reassert his authority by choosing a new might-makes-right White House chief of staff who has said that “the real world” is “governed by power.” In recent days, his secretaries of state and defense have questioned the extent that international laws apply to “men with swords,” which is, of course, how Mr. Trump and his testosterone-promoting team see themselves.

“The presidency, our presidency, is considered a strong presidency. You can do a lot,” Mr. Trump told CBS News on election night as voters were rejecting Republicans across the country, handing control of both houses of Congress to Democrats. Speaking with Fox News in Shenzhen on Thursday before his meetings, Mr. Trump emphasized that he will defy the new Congress. “They could do all the bills they want,” he said. “I just go veto, veto, veto.”

Unpopular presidents who lose control of Congress often turn to international affairs where they have more latitude to operate. Mr. Trump did not need congressional approval to meet with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. But with his Iran war stalled after nine months, Mr. Trump has less room to maneuver. And foreign leaders understand that he is now a lame duck who will be out of office in just over two years.

But the summit offered a welcome respite to Mr. Trump, who has long expressed admiration for authoritarian leaders like Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi, often applying the word “strong” to them, perhaps his favorite compliment. He has over the years talked enviously of their ability to get things done unburdened by the messy obstacles of legislatures and courts.

Indeed, Mr. Putin later suggested that he and Mr. Trump shared a common view of “civilizational values” and a “certain closeness” in perspectives. “For instance,” Mr. Putin told reporters after the meeting, “we were just discussing issues of democracy, right? But what is democracy, really?” He went on to suggest that “is, in fact, a liberal attempt to monopolize power — a liberal dictatorship, if you will.”

In his second term, Mr. Trump has endeavored to assert executive power to a far greater degree than in his first, asserting authority to sidestep Congress and the courts. He has taken an expansive view of his office, using the Justice Department to prosecute his personal enemies, gutting congressionally authorized agencies, firing theoretically independent officials and so on.

Asked in an interview with The New York Times in January whether he acknowledged any limits to his global power, he said: “Yeah, there is one thing. My own morality. My own mind. It’s the only thing that can stop me.”

Last month, he mused out loud to reporters in the Oval Office about how he could have used his power to go after Democrats like former Presidents Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Barack Obama and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, but chose not to. “I can do whatever I want, if I want,” he said.

Mr. Trump’s view of power goes back to his days in business. As a family-owned firm, the Trump Organization had no board of directors or shareholders to whom Mr. Trump had to answer. His decisions essentially were the final word. After he was inaugurated for his first term in 2017, he expressed shock that the government did not operate the same way.

He has surrounded himself with advisers who share his view of power, and his choice of chief of staff after his party’s disastrous midterm results made clear that he has no intention of backing down.

Stephen Miller, the new chief, has long voiced maximalist ideas about executive power. As a policy aide in the first Trump administration, Mr. Miller responded to a judge’s ruling striking down a ban on people from predominantly Muslim countries by saying that “the powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned.”

In January, he dismissed talk of international law in discussing Mr. Trump’s desire to take control of Greenland. “We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” Mr. Miller told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.”

Some other Trump advisers have worried Mr. Miller was going too far. As part of the president’s mass deportation blitz, Mr. Miller last year suggested suspending the constitutional right of habeas corpus and invoking the Insurrection Act to deploy the military to American streets in response to protests.

Will Scharf, then the staff secretary and now the White House counsel, wrote confidential memos objecting to both ideas, according to “Regime Change,” the recent book by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan of The Times. Both ideas were eventually put to the side, but never definitively ruled out.

But it is not as if Mr. Scharf is a dove when it comes to assertion of presidential power. Last week, he sent Democrats in Congress a letter warning that their efforts to investigate the Trump administration could be interpreted as intimidation and “may cross the line into blatant criminality” and “warrant further investigation.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio reflected the administration’s view about the reach of its authority during a recent speech to the Federalist Society denouncing the International Criminal Court, an institution that the United States has never joined but has become a particular target of Mr. Trump lately. Among other things, the court has issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Putin for alleged war crimes stemming from his invasion of Ukraine.

“If they’re foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans,” Mr. Rubio said of the international court, “our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions. He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

“Not politically correct to say that,” he added, “but that’s what he said. That’s what he said.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth liked the idea so much that he posted a clip of Mr. Rubio online along with the line: “Stop quoting laws to MEN WITH SWORDS.”

If Mr. Rubio was making a somewhat nuanced argument that the international court’s jurisdiction — its “paper decrees” — did not apply to the United States, Mr. Hegseth seemed to take it one step further, disdaining the very idea of laws constraining military action.

Mr. Hegseth’s post generated criticism even from fellow conservatives who oppose American recognition of the International Criminal Court. Former Representative Justin Amash of Michigan, who left the Republican Party, called it an abandonment of the rule of law.

“Rejecting the ICC’s jurisdiction is one thing,” he wrote online. “Declaring that laws become irrelevant the moment swords appear is another. That’s just ‘might makes right,’ which is a fundamental rejection of both Christian ethics and America’s founding.”

In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin made clear where they stood on the idea of the reach of international law. In the joint statement they released afterward, they said that immunity of state officials is “of paramount importance.” On that, at least, the leaders of America, China and Russia were on the same page.

item.title: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
item.description:
President Trump used his first-ever trilateral summit with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Thursday to say that their respective nations were “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth.”

But after an 80-minute conversation at a lakeside villa in the city of Shenzhen, a Chinese technology hub, it was unclear whether the three leaders had agreed to return to the kind of arms control talks that for decades were a centerpiece of diplomacy among superpowers during the Cold War. On new threats, including artificial intelligence, the three leaders were largely silent.

Mr. Trump, who also met with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin separately at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum this week, appeared delighted to convene the world’s largest nuclear powers for a discussion about disarmament. But he did not come with a detailed plan for how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons, or outline a path to one.

Instead, Mr. Trump relished what amounted to a high-profile photo opportunity of the three leaders seated around a circular wooden table. For Mr. Trump, the main achievement seemed to be a mutual commitment to keep talking about peace — without taking meaningful steps toward it.

“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite.” Mr. Trump told Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.”

While China, which has the fastest-growing nuclear arsenal on earth, agreed to participate in the three-way discussion of nuclear weapons, the leaders announced little concrete beyond agreeing to continue a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. Mr. Xi has long been reluctant to agree to nuclear arms control because China’s arsenal remains a fraction the size of those belonging to Russia and the United States.

In the end, Mr. Trump’s whirlwind journey — two weeks after the Republican Party suffered a wipeout in the midterm elections and amid anxiety at home about widespread digital outages — amounted to a grand show of camaraderie.

As host of the tightly choreographed event, Mr. Xi flattered Mr. Trump and gave him an opportunity to ask for China’s assistance on matters ranging from ending global conflicts to spending more on U.S. agricultural goods. The summit also removed Mr. Putin from his status a global pariah over his invasion of Ukraine, elevating him to a leader deserving of equal diplomatic footing.

But for all of the talk of peace, there was no announcement of breakthroughs in the talks the Trump administration is engaged in to end that conflict. Nor did Mr. Trump appear to dwell on finding a way out of the its war with Iran.

“We don’t need any help,” Mr. Trump said, when asked by a Fox News reporter before the summit whether he would seek assistance from the other leaders in ending a conflict of his own making. In fact, the help Mr. Trump could ask for would involve demanding that China and Russia stop assisting Iran: U.S. intelligence has concluded that both countries provided either technology or targeting information that likely helped the Iranians strike American military bases in the Middle East.

On Fox News, Mr. Trump described the three-way conversation as a way to disrupt the growing “partnership without limits” that Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin say they have formed in recent years. Mr. Trump said that he hoped to break up that alignment and turn it into a three-way conversation, rather than a partnership focused on countering American influence.

China and Russia’s alignment, Mr. Trump said, “should have never been allowed to happen.”

Seeking his own path into Mr. Xi’s good graces, Mr. Trump has held three meetings with the Chinese leader this year, with the goal of cooling a tit-for-tat trade war and of building up a personal relationship through mutual flattery. Mr. Trump traveled to Joint Base Andrews to welcome Mr. Xi to Washington in May, and Mr. Xi responded in kind when Mr. Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, treating the president to a military exercise and a fleet of U.S. and Chinese flag-waving dancers in a flurry of pink, blue and white outfits.

In Shenzhen, the heart of China’s robotics, telecommunications, semiconductor and software industries, Mr. Trump did not visit the chief technological competitors to the United States, or see coffee-serving robots near the city’s center.

Still, he marveled over the ceremonial welcome and held it up as evidence of a warming bond, telling an interviewer that “one of the great presidents of China” had greeted him. “He’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Mr. Trump said.

The president, who spends much of his time in the United States on bombastic appearances and incendiary social media posts, was on his best behavior alongside Mr. Xi. (He was his old self on Fox News before the summit, when he threatened to wipe out Iran should it attack the United States directly.)

Mr. Xi, for his part, said a much improved relationship between China and the United States in recent months was “the right way” for the two powers to “get along.” But he also warned that the key to keeping ties stable “lies in taking concrete actions to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state.” The remarks came days after Washington moved to close a loophole on Chinese access to advanced A.I. chips.

As for Mr. Putin, the summit was his first encounter with Mr. Trump since the two men met in Alaska last year. That meeting was a diplomatic flop, and the war in Ukraine has intensified since then. The peace mechanism Mr. Trump advocated — a direct meeting between Mr. Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, moderated by Mr. Trump — has yet to materialize.

This time, White House officials were modest in their predictions. Expectations were set so low that White House officials who previewed the trip last week initially said that Mr. Trump would not bring up the war in Ukraine at all, although he ultimately did.

In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump continued welcoming Russia back into the fold of great superpowers. He called Mr. Putin “my friend,” and insisted that all three leaders would like to see the war end quickly. The Russian leader reiterated after the meeting, however, that he would not be negotiating with Ukraine.

During the trilateral meeting, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin embraced the idea of peaceful leadership, without making commitments that would be much of a burden to either of their countries. In his own remarks, Mr. Putin said that their nations were “united not only by the status of being the victorious countries in World War II, but most importantly by the joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.”

And Mr. Xi mentioned a utopian goal that has pretty much fallen off the agenda of superpowers. He described nuclear weapons as a “sword of Damocles hanging over humanity” that should be eliminated. But Beijing has typically called on the United States to take the first steps in arms control, a demand that Mr. Trump seemed to acknowledge earlier in the day.

“For me, it’s a hard thing,” he told Fox News. “And it’s probably hard for them to do also.”

It has been done before, by Mr. Trump’s predecessors. Today, the United States and Russia each have slightly more than 5,000 nuclear warheads, and only 1,550 deployed under the New Start treaty that expired earlier this year — down from tens of thousands on both sides during the Cold War.

China, however, was never a party to past nuclear reduction treaties, and it is now intent on building up to at least current Russian and U.S. levels.

Mr. Trump also said in Shenzen that he wanted to crack down on nuclear proliferation by smaller powers — his justification for attacking Iran — and restrain what he said were the excesses of “rogue” organizations like the International Criminal Court.

Mr. Putin is subject to an I.C.C. arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Nevertheless Mr. Trump welcomed the Russian leader in Alaska last year and extending an invitation to the Group of 20 summit next month in Florida. Mr. Putin told reporters after the meeting that he was unsure if he would attend.

One topic that went missing from each leader’s remarks was artificial intelligence, as China and the United States are locked in fierce competition over the new technology.

Mr. Trump did not answer a question, shouted by a Bloomberg News reporter at APEC earlier in the day, if the former chief executive of Nvidia — a company that has been central to the A.I. boom — had been disloyal to the United States. The executive, Jensen Huang, resigned after he was found to have two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset.

The reporter who shouted the question was admonished by Chinese officials and barred from the trilateral meeting. Mr. Trump seemed blasé about the matter of espionage earlier in the day, telling Fox News that “we spy on them too.”

As the president basked in flattery from an authoritarian whose iron-fisted leadership he has openly admired, he gently suggested that he had not received as much media coverage as he would have liked.

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it,” Mr. Trump said of his trip.

David Pierson contributed reporting.
