item.title: U.S. Auctions 31.5 Million Acres of Pacific Ocean to Deep Sea Mining Company
item.description:
In the first sale of its kind, the Trump administration on Thursday leased 31.5 million acres of the Pacific Ocean to a private deep sea mining company, despite a judge’s ruling this week that the auction would be illegal.

Only one firm bid to lease the seabed, which sits off American Samoa. The $6 million lease would allow the company to do mapping and other preliminary work but not actually mine the ocean floor for metals and minerals.

Administration officials would not disclose the identity of the successful bidder, saying it would be publicly released on Friday.

But Impossible Metals, a San Diego-based deep sea mining firm, had asked the government in April to hold the commercial auction. Company officials did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

The auction took place in Thousand Oaks, Calif., at a fire station near the regional office of the Marine Minerals Administration, a branch of the Interior Department that was created in July. Only two bidders showed up.

Outside the fire station, protesters marched and carried signs opposing the sale.

Deep-sea mining would involve scooping up nodules found on the seafloor that are rich in metals like cobalt, nickel, and manganese, which are important to manufacturing electric cars, batteries and other clean-energy technologies.

But mining the deep ocean has raised global opposition, and environmentalists argue that underwater plumes of sediment stirred up by mining machinery could devastate deep sea ecosystems.

More than 45 countries have called for a ban or pause on seabed mining, which currently does not exist in any commercial form.

But deep sea mining is a priority for President Trump, who last April signed an executive order that instructed the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to expedite approvals for mining companies.

Trump administration officials said the sale would benefit U.S. industries that rely on critical minerals.

“This sale is a critical first step in our offshore energy strategy,” said Michael Olsen, acting director of the Marine Minerals Administration. “It allows us to learn more about the resources in our offshore federal waters, and it enables us to assess whether those resources could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

Whoever the winning bidder is might face an extended legal fight to start prospecting for those deep sea nodules.

On Monday, Judge Jill Otake of the U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii ruled that the National Marine Fisheries Service “did not even attempt to consider” the potential harms to endangered marine species when it approved the planned sale, violating the Endangered Species Act. Mr. Trump nominated Judge Otake to the bench in 2017.

The proposed mining area is adjacent to the Rose Atoll National Marine Monument, a 13,500-square mile protected area known for its fragile pink-colored coral reefs, nesting areas for sea turtles, whales and other marine mammals, and more than 250 species of fish and seabirds.

Environmental groups said that the winner of the bid will face difficulty in pursuing a lease that has been ruled unlawful.

“There are a lot of problems with this sale,” said Erik Van de Stouwe, senior attorney for the Natural Resources Defense Council. “The investors of this bidder should ask a lot of hard questions given the court’s recent ruling.”

The N.R.D.C., Earthjustice and Finafinau, a youth-group based in American Samoa, sued the Marine Minerals Administration on Wednesday in federal court in Hawaii, asking the court to strike down any leases that the agency awards.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, said that although the mining lease is outside territorial waters of American Samoa, mining on the seafloor will stir up sediment and other pollution that spreads beyond the immediate area.

“We’re talking about sediment plumes, we’re talking about impacts on marine ecosystems that we completely don’t understand,” Ms. Suluai-Mahuka said in an interview. “How is that going to affect our corals. How is that going to affect other ecosystems that are already in place?”

Suluai-Mahuka said that many of the 49,000 island residents depend on the commercial tuna industry for their livelihood. They also depend on the ocean for their food. Both are at risk from commercial mining activity, she said.

“At a basic family level, we depend on whether or not we can feed ourselves from the ocean,” Ms. Suluai-Mahuka said. “You will see families fishing often, and eating the fish that they catch — it’s a daily way of people being able to feed their families. That hasn’t actually been factored in, either.”

American Samoa banned deep sea mining in 2024, citing “significant risks” to marine biodiversity, however its elected officials are split on the issue. On Monday, Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, a Republican, said he supported the sale.

“Today, we stand at the threshold of a new era of exploration, one that could unlock scientific knowledge, create economic opportunities, and strengthen American Samoa’s role in America’s strategic future in the Pacific,” the governor said in a statement.

Delegate Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen, a Republican who represents the U.S. territory in the U.S. House, called the Monday ruling against the sale “significant” and said that she would reintroduce legislation to ban deep sea mining near American Samoa.

“We treasure our beautiful shores and waters, and we rely on a healthy ocean for fishing,” Ms. Radewagen said in an email to The Times.

item.title: Love and Carjackings in a Video Game
item.description:
Full disclosure: I don’t play video games. I have never played video games. I did read a novel about video games once! (“Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow,” by Gabrielle Zevin. It’s good.)

But even I haven’t been able to avoid the cultural juggernaut that is Grand Theft Auto VI. This week, the legendary franchise released a new game after a 13-year hiatus, and it’s fair to characterize the response as rapturous. “The most extraordinary game I’ve ever reviewed,” one critic said. “The year’s signature cultural event,” one of our reporters wrote. Some are expecting the first week’s sales to approach $2 billion. “G.T.A. flu” — people planning to stay home from work or school to play — is a thing.

And so I called up my colleague Zachary Small, who reports on arts and culture (and also plays Grand Theft Auto). I wanted to ask him about the blockbuster cultural phenomenon known as G.T.A.

Zach, I am possibly the farthest thing from this game’s target audience. So explain to me: What’s the deal with Grand Theft Auto?

Today we think of Grand Theft Auto as very American, but it actually has roots in Scotland. It was this British take, in the form of a video game, on American crime movies — but the creators realized it’s a lot more fun to play as the bad guys than the good guys.

The Grand Theft Auto we know today unleashes players to wreak havoc across various fictional cities. You can steal cars. You can run over pedestrians. You can do a drug deal or get into a shootout with the police.

So what’s fun about it is that you can do crazy stuff that you can’t do in real life?

You’re thinking about it in the right way. But if you want a more philosophical spin on it, you could say that Grand Theft Auto is also commentary — that it offers this kind of satirical perspective on American culture, and what it means to try to achieve the American dream.

[Our colleague Joseph Bernstein has a great piece about how G.T.A. has always been a cartoonish parody of the United States — and how reality has now outrun the joke.]

Historically, there’s been a lot of pushback from educators and politicians against G.T.A. What were they worried about?

So a lot of the initial controversy around Grand Theft Auto was the developers’ own doing. It’s been reported that when the original came out in 1997, they paid P.R. companies to reach out to British tabloids and say, “Boy, this is a really controversial game; it’s super violent.” And, of course, that had the effect of making people want to play.

But later on, in the post-9/11 period, there were these fears about whether we’d become a violent society. And a lot of those fears became focused on video games and specifically Grand Theft Auto. And it became this sort of moral panic, based on research that today has been largely debunked.

You don’t really hear much of this in the response to G.T.A. VI.

Right, and I think that’s because this release comes at a moment when gaming as an industry is a lot more respected. The game is set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City, and real elected officials in Miami are totally embracing it. The last time a G.T.A. was set in Vice City, there were protests and a lawsuit in Miami. So, there’s been this complete 180.

Why is that?

The series has been around for almost 30 years. A lot of people, including government officials, grew up playing these games, and feel nostalgia for them.

The game itself has also matured in this latest release. G.T.A. had been criticized for misogyny; one of the lead characters this time is a woman who is just as complex as her male counterpart. There’s romance. And, in addition to carjacking people, you can have your character engage in home repairs. So that’s one part of it.

The other part is the quality of these games, which is undeniable. The detail and the realism of G.T.A. VI is incredible.

Think about it this way. This game involves a lot of walking on the beach. Now think about how your foot hits the sand when you’re walking on the beach and how all the tiny pebbles move around as a result. For an animator, how many hours of work does that take? How much work just so a character can lean against a wall? Think about the physics of the clothes a character is wearing as he leans.

Now, think about the fact that in G.T.A. VI, you can go to the beach, and see different scenes unfolding everywhere you look. You can see a dog running into a wave. You can see people hitting a beach ball back and forth. And all of it looks incredibly realistic. The amount of work that takes cannot be overstated. All these thousands of tiny details have been taken into account by a team of almost 5,000 people, with a budget of more than $1 billion.

A huge amount of money and time went into G.T.A. VI. It’s also expected to generate huge sales. Where does the gaming industry go from here?

Yes, it’s going to make record amounts of money. But virtually no other studio in the video game industry could spend the money and time Rockstar Games took to make it. That was a huge risk. It’s going to be a hit, but that’s not a very sustainable approach. Imagine putting in that kind of investment and winding up with a flop. It’s hard to imagine we’re going to see many more of these sorts of prestige releases.

Are you going to play it?

I started this morning! So far I’ve gotten into a shootout, fenced some acid, and, of course, committed grand theft auto.

President Trump called Russia’s leader, Vladimir Putin, his “friend,” gushed about “making history,” and said the U.S., China and Russia should discuss reducing their nuclear weapons. But after the leaders of those countries held their first-ever trilateral summit, there were no breakthroughs on nuclear weapons, the war in Ukraine or confronting threats from A.I.

There is also little chance that the meeting will change the basic worldview of Putin and China’s leader, Xi Jinping. My colleague Edward Wong writes that Putin and Xi share a vision of transforming the world order by usurping the role of the United States as the sole superpower.

Anthropic had a roller-coaster first day on the stock market. Its shares surged more than 30 percent only to give up much of those gains, but it was still the biggest I.P.O. in history. The A.I. company is now worth about $2 trillion.

My tech reporter colleague Cory Weinberg explains in the video below how Anthropic’s stock market debut could affect its attempt to prioritize A.I. safety over profits.

The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims when, in a few weeks in 2017, it killed at least 10,000 people and forced three-quarters of a million people to flee.

An aerial attack by Yemen’s Houthi militia damaged the Riyadh skyscraper housing the offices of Saudi Arabia’s $900 billion sovereign wealth fund.

Around 92,000 people are attending the U.N. climate conference, which has ballooned into a trade show and networking opportunity, but the end result is expected to be modest.

Sitting on the Eurostar from London to Paris this week, the English Channel above me, I was hit by a wave of nostalgia.

After I moved from London to Paris in my early 20s, I took the Eurostar all the time. It all felt so familiar: the British and European sockets side by side, the Cheddar sandwiches and Perrier on the menu, the multilingual train personnel.

This was pre-Brexit, a time when Brits, like other Europeans, could just move to another European country and live and work there. Young Brits today can’t do what I did — or at least not as easily. (Young Europeans can’t easily move to Britain, either, but they still have the other E.U. countries to pick from.) Whatever you think about Brexit, one thing is worth noting: Young people voted overwhelmingly against it.

Young people frustrated at their lack of political power, especially in aging societies, have been a running theme in the news recently.

At the time of the Brexit referendum, a British friend told me that her dad, then in his 70s, had called her to ask how he should vote. He said he was in favor of Britain’s leaving, but realized this would affect her and her children more, and felt obliged to give her his vote.

I remembered that story when a French friend, whose teenage daughter is among the protesters at her Parisian high school, also said he would let her decide whom he should vote for in next year’s presidential election. “It’s about her future more than mine,” he said.

As it happens, my colleague Amelia Nierenberg is working on a story about Gen Z’s political hopes and dreams. If you’re 18 to 29, write to her here.

In the meantime, this week’s song is a bilingual collab between Zaho de Sagazan (French) and Tom Odell (British) called “Old Friend.” I love it.

Bon weekend! — Katrin

item.title: Unexpected Fallout From the Iran War
item.description:
Early this year, the start of the war in Iran caused what the International Energy Agency called “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.”

Now, months later, the agency says some of the changes are permanent.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” the I.E.A. executive director, Fatih Birol, said in a statement today alongside the organization’s annual World Energy Outlook.

My colleague Lisa Friedman wrote about the main takeaways for global energy markets. In short: Electrification is accelerating, drivers outside the United States are shifting rapidly to electric vehicles, and the extent to which the disruption reshapes energy policies will depend a lot on how long it lasts.

All of those changes have huge consequences for greenhouse gas emissions. So today, I’ll dive into the report’s climate implications.

The war in Iran has driven up gas and diesel prices around the world, making electric vehicles a more appealing and cost-competitive option. Globally, more than a quarter of the passenger cars sold this year will be full-electric or hybrid, the World Energy Outlook predicts. Electric vehicle sales have more than doubled in India, Australia and Brazil over the past year.

The United States has not kept up with the trend — E.V.s made up about 6 percent of domestic light-duty vehicle sales in the first eight months of the year, according to an analysis by the research group Ember. That adoption rate has been surpassed by 49 of the 56 countries where Ember tracks E.V. markets.

The report also finds that China is making real progress in electrifying heavy trucks. I wrote this year that electric big rigs have been slow to take off, largely because of high costs and charging obstacles.

In China, sales of electric trucks now make up about 35 percent of the new truck market, a rapid increase driven by government incentives and a business model that makes them more affordable.

Instead of buying trucks equipped with permanent batteries that need to be recharged periodically, operators in China are buying vehicles with batteries that can be swapped in a few minutes at roadside stations.

“You don’t have to pay for the expensive part of the truck, which is the battery,” said Dave Jones, chief analyst at Ember.

At the start of the war, a flurry of developments suggested that spiking prices for oil and gas imports could drive countries to embrace coal as a replacement.

Japan, Korea and Thailand delayed scheduled coal plant retirements and returned idle units to service. Italy postponed a planned phaseout. In September, my colleague Brad Plumer reported that the world was on track to burn record amounts of coal this year, largely because of fossil fuel shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

When burned, coal produces more planet-warming greenhouse gases than any other energy source.

The new I.E.A. analysis finds that the coal surge is temporary. It forecasts that coal use will be in decline globally by 2030 in all of the report’s projected scenarios.

The disruption of global oil and gas flows has caused countries that import energy to focus on producing more at home, the report found.

“The focus at the moment is just how expensive oil and gas is,” Mr. Jones said. “So everyone is trying to do whatever they can to replace oil and gas.”

In most places, that pivot is a boon for renewables and nuclear power.

“Encouragingly for the future, energy security and energy transitions have never been so closely aligned,” Mr. Birol said.

The I.E.A. modeled a range of scenarios for the future of oil and gas. Even in the one based on longer-term disruption of global oil and gas flows, the world is a long way from cutting emissions enough to keep average global temperatures below the threshold of 2 degrees Celsius that was established in the 2015 Paris Agreement, let alone the pact’s more ambitious 1.5-degree aspirational goal. The report also found that data centers could double global electricity use by 2030.

What does a video game need to accurately reflect America today? Sex. Violence. Phones. Drugs. Class struggle.

Grand Theft Auto VI, which came out this week, has all that. It also has finely realized depictions of every kind of extreme weather that is becoming more common because of climate change.

In Leonida, the game’s fictional world, which is modeled on Florida, there are tropical storms, torrential downpours, heavy winds and swampy afternoons. The game is also getting high marks for accurately representing biodiversity: There are manatees, alligators and 62 species of birds, including flamingos, gulls and pelicans.

While the weather doesn’t affect the plot of the game, it adds to the verisimilitude of G.T.A., and conjures a mood that, at times, is appropriately apocalyptic.

To better understand the environment in Leonida, I called my colleague Joseph Bernstein, who had early access to the game and spent the better part of the last month rampaging through Vice City.

Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

What’s the weather like in Leonida?

You can feel the humidity. It has that distinct quality to the air. You can smell the sea breeze, but it’s also like your shirt is sticking to your torso and you feel that.

How does the weather shape the atmosphere of the game?

One of the themes of the game is obviously excess. You are existing in this kind of heightened fun house, an over-the-top place. And the fact that Florida is beset by over-the-top weather that is obviously exacerbated by climate change is clearly part of the whole deal.

Previous installments of G.T.A. satirized America, and this one is much more realistic. How does the weather play into that?

It’s a part of the world that can’t be ignored. To not have it would be an oversight. You need it. It’s part of existence.

Interviewed by David Gelles

item.title: Body Bags and War on ‘Wokismo’: A President’s First 100 Days
item.description:
When Abelardo De La Espriella was a lawyer representing accused drug traffickers and money launderers, he said he only took cases so contentious that they gave him vertigo.

In his first 100 days as Colombia’s president, he has shown a similar appetite for controversy.

Following a lethal operation against an armed group, he posed with body bags, ignored the resulting outcry, fought a judge’s order and went on posting images of body bags online. He has also made a routine of confronting men captured in police or military raids and berating them on camera.

The Colombian president’s moves have inspired comparisons to Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian leader, whose slick productions showing off his hard-line security strategy Mr. De La Espriella seems determined to outdo.

His actions have drawn praise and sharp rebukes.

Former Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos, who received the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize for a peace accord that ended a decades-long conflict with the country’s largest rebel group, warned that Mr. De La Espriella could drag Colombia back into the past.

Supporters, however, have cheered his frontal attack on criminal groups, which many felt had been allowed to run rampant under the previous, leftist president, Gustavo Petro, and have celebrated Mr. De La Espriella as “the body bagger.”

Lorena Angarita, 53, who runs a communications workers’ association in Bogotá, said the president had “saved Colombia from imminent disaster.’’

About half of Colombians are “very offended” by the president’s theatrics, said Camilo Restrepo, 52, an artist in Medellín, and half are “very excited.”

The president’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. De La Espriella, 48, had never held public office before June, when he was endorsed by President Trump and elected in a runoff against a left-wing rival, by less than a percentage point. Experts say his actions as president have done little to unify the polarized population, deepening division instead.

“He is sticking to what worked for him in the campaign,” said Ángel Beccassino, a political strategist who wrote a book about Mr. De La Espriella.

Like other conservatives elected recently in Latin America, Mr. De La Espriella seized on voters’ fears over security and borrowed culture-war tactics from Mr. Trump.

As president, he has declared an “open and all-out war on wokismo.”

In October, the government removed dozens of works from the National Museum, including feminist, L.G.B.T.Q. and political pieces — then sent riot police to quash protests. (Complying with a judge’s order, the government later returned the works.)

The government also recently opened an investigation into Mr. Petro, over accusations that he gave government contracts to women he met on sex websites. Mr. Petro has denied the claims.

Sandra Borda, a Colombian political scientist, said the new government is advancing the values agenda that Mr. De La Espriella promised the religious right.

The president is also testing out the Trump strategy of “flooding the zone” — doing “something every day to dominate the news cycle,” she said, “so you have everyone talking about one thing, while you’re doing another.”

But Colombians are not so easily distracted, Ms. Borda said.

At the 100-day mark, many are concerned over how an “outsider” government will handle a budget deficit that ballooned under Mr. Petro.

The De La Espriella government’s proposed tax hikes face stiff opposition from conservatives in Colombia’s Congress; its proposed cuts to social spending have prompted left-wing opponents to call for nationwide protests.

Thousands of Colombians affected by Mr. Petro’s stalled health care overhaul are still waiting for the fixes that the new president had promised within 90 days, including restoring access to medicine and care.

And some victims of the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck days after he took office are still clamoring for rent relief.

Óscar Montes, a Colombian political analyst who published a book of interviews with Mr. De La Espriella, compared the president to a person “arriving to a house someone else lived in,” and finding “it’s been destroyed from the inside.”

He said the problems left behind by Mr. Petro would require time to tackle and stabilize.

By early November, the new president’s approval rating had slipped modestly, to 48.7 percent, from 51.8 percent in August, according to an AtlasIntel poll for Bloomberg.

The clear focus of Mr. De La Espriella’s first 100 days has been his security strategy, which keeps him crisscrossing the country.

In online videos, he has patrolled a city at night with a gun on his hip, defying an armed group’s lockdown order. He has appeared to give commands over a walkie-talkie and announced operations with names like Mano de Hierro, or Iron Hand. He has autographed a bomb about to be dropped on an enemy camp.

The Trump administration is pursuing a military response to drug trafficking in Latin America and has focused on Colombia, the world’s largest cocaine producer.

Mr. De La Espriella has been eager to cooperate. He disputed a New York Times report that he had told Washington he didn’t have enough support in Colombia’s Congress to authorize joint military strikes; his foreign minister said the government hoped the move would “quickly” pass in Congress.

At Washington’s urging, Mr. De La Espriella has also moved to restart aerial fumigation of coca, cocaine’s base ingredient, though Colombia’s courts have pushed back.

Nearly every day, the president has announced another “major blow” against crime: arrests, raids, drug and weapons seizures. He has signed nearly 170 extradition orders — with a Sharpie, in a seeming nod to Mr. Trump.

Analysts say Mr. De La Espriella has been emboldened by Washington’s anti-trafficking push, but warn that the offensive could spiral.

Unlike Mr. Bukele of El Salvador, who ordered mass arrests to pacify a compact country of six million, Mr. De La Espriella presides over a large nation with more than 54 million people. Armed groups control significant swaths of territory, financed by cocaine and illicit gold and equipped with lethal drones.

“The military offensive is undeniably having an impact on the number of arrests and operations,” said Jorge Mantilla, a Colombian conflict analyst. “But, so far, it has not translated into greater territorial control, or a reduction in violence, or a defeat of those groups.”

The groups are also starting to hit back, stirring fears of a return to tit-for-tat violence with the state. More than three dozen soldiers and police have been killed since August, according to officials, including in a recent drone strike on a base.

Mr. De La Espriella has become the face of the military offensive.

Many say that is the work of Carlos Suárez, a strategist who steered his campaign. Like Mr. De La Espriella, Mr. Suárez was a lawyer who spent years in Miami and represented high-profile Colombians facing charges in the United States.

Mr. Suárez is shaping the government’s anti-woke campaign, officials have said, and influenced the recent replacement of a moderate interior minister with a religious hard-liner.

He is also behind the videos chronicling the security offensive, which have grown bolder by the week. Mr. De La Espriella has gone from khakis and baseball cap to full camouflage and beret.

Mr. Suárez did not respond to a request for comment.

Juan Nicolás Garzón, a Colombian political scientist, said that “the sight of a president with a pistol on his belt, in uniform,” gives Colombians a sense that their leader is taking charge of security down to “the micro level.”

But Mr. Becassino, who wrote about Mr. De La Espriella years ago, said his strategist was pushing him toward “grandstanding and spectacle, costume changes and bombastic posturing,” adding, “They’re using that to cover up the lack of results.”

María Jimena Duzán, a prominent Colombian journalist and commentator, said the strategy could endanger the president’s credibility abroad, making him look “like a cartoonish strongman dressed up like a soldier.”

Eligio Montes, 55, a handyman in Cartagena, said he voted for Mr. De La Espriella “because he said he would finish off the criminals.” But he was not entirely convinced by what he had seen, he said.

“They say it is pure show.”

Still, by one measure, the strategy has succeeded. After just 100 days, Mr. De La Espriella has become a phenomenon, the latest vivid figure to emerge on the global right. He has inspired memes, parodies, Halloween costumes and imitation by other leaders.

Traffickers have taken notice, too. In October, when the authorities in Costa Rica seized some 250 bricks of cocaine, they found his photograph stuck on every one.

Simón Posada contributed reporting from Bogotá and Cartagena, Colombia.

item.title: A Village Burned, Its People Killed or Exiled. Was It Genocide?
item.description:
As his village burned, Mustafa Kamal somehow kept his family safe.

Husband and wife, three sons, three daughters, a granddaughter, they ran until their breath ran out. They stumbled past bodies of people they knew, shot by Myanmar’s security forces. They slogged through mud that claimed some of their clothes and trekked over jungle passes thick with leeches. Days later, when they finally crossed a river into Bangladesh, they rowed past swollen bodies of other Rohingya Muslims who never made it to the other side alive.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice in The Hague is ruling whether the atrocities against the Rohingya ethnic minority constitute a genocide waged by the Myanmar state. The killing, gang rape and mass arson reached a furious zenith in 2017, building on years of systematic persecution. Three quarters of a million Rohingya flooded into Bangladesh in a matter of weeks, the most rapid refugee exodus in recent history. And more kept coming.

A judgment in a country half a world away would matter, Mr. Kamal told me. It would acknowledge the fate of his home, Zammona, one of 400 Rohingya villages that were obliterated by Myanmar security forces nine years ago.

But sitting in the dark, cramped shelter that is now his home in Bangladesh, part of what is now the world’s largest refugee settlement, Mr. Kamal said that the trauma did not end nine years ago. For the Rohingya, he said, misery never ends.

International aid to the camps has plummeted. Hunger and disease are rampant. In May, Mr. Kamal’s 18-year-old son was killed by Rohingya militants who have unleashed a reign of terror in the refugee camps. Human traffickers roam the narrow spaces between tarpaulin shelters, grabbing men, women and children. One of Mr. Kamal’s daughters was kidnapped by a militant, who forced himself on her. She had no choice but to marry him, and they now have a baby boy.

“Oh, Allah, why is there no justice for the Rohingya anywhere on earth?” Mr. Kamal said, weeping as he clutched a photo of his dead son.

Mr. Kamal, now 66, grew up in Zammona, a fertile collection of hamlets in Myanmar’s far west, dotted with fish ponds, well-stocked groceries and mosques with graceful arches. His father was a teacher at a government school. Mr. Kamal learned Burmese, the language of Myanmar’s Buddhist Bamar majority, and took a job as a trader, ferrying goods from one town to another. His wife, Toyuba Khatun, was educated, too.

The Rohingya had long faced repression from the military, which ruled Myanmar for decades and preserved power for the Bamar. In the 1980s, the Rohingya lost their legal status in Myanmar, their citizenship essentially stripped from them. Babies rarely were issued birth certificates. There was also occasional tension with the Rakhine ethnic group, with whom the Rohingya shared Rakhine State.

Still, Mr. Kamal said he had easy relations with Rakhine villagers who lived nearby. After all, he had gone to school with them; his father had been their teacher.

A store owner in Zammona, Mohammed Yunus said he welcomed Buddhist customers, bantering with them as they haggled over the latest clothes or electronics. (Zammona is called Zin Paing Nyar in the Burmese language.)

In 2012, violence flared between the Rohingya and the Rakhine, inflamed by state media coverage. Gatherings of more than five Rohingya were banned. Mosques were shuttered. Many Rohingya children no longer felt welcome at government schools. Mr. Kamal’s father secretly taught his grandchildren at home, desperate for the next generation to be educated.

When Mr. Kamal’s daughter Rehana Bibi got married, a Myanmar official forbade her from having more than two children. A false narrative took hold across Myanmar that the high birthrate of Rohingya was part of a global Muslim plot to swamp Buddhist lands. Military propaganda inaccurately portrayed the Rohingya as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. Never mind that Rohingya had been elected to Parliament, studied at the nation’s finest universities, and once enjoyed government radio broadcasts in their own language, just like any other of the nation’s many ethnic groups. In the 2015 elections, which elevated the party of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, the Nobel Peace laureate, the Rohingya lost their right to vote.

On Oct. 9, 2016, a militant group led by a Rohingya refugee who was born in Pakistan and schooled in Saudi Arabia launched attacks on Myanmar security outposts, killing nine police officers, according to the Myanmar authorities.

The security forces’ response to the attacks punished an entire ethnicity.

In Zammona, Mr. Kamal locked the door to his spacious wooden house and prayed with his family that the soldiers would not attack.

Over the next few months, soldiers rounded up men in Zammona, accusing them of participating in the militant raids, charges they denied. Their only crime, they said, was being young, able-bodied Rohingya men. One was given a 54-year prison sentence. Soyadul Amin and Abdul Rohim were sentenced to 16 years each. Mr. Amin described how the Myanmar soldiers tied his arms behind his back, threw him on the ground and laughed as they ordered him to lap up his food like an animal. When he and others cried out for water, the soldiers offered urine.

The United Nations said at the time that hundreds of Rohingya were killed and that the crackdown “very likely” constituted crimes against humanity.

“We could not imagine what would happen next,” Mr. Kamal said. “Our people, our Rohingya were finished.”

On Aug. 25, 2017, the Rohingya militants carried out another series of attacks, killing more than a dozen security forces. This time, the military was prepared. Within hours, the scorched-earth retribution began.

Mr. Kamal heard the rocket launchers crescendo from the east. He gathered his family, but there was no time to grab anything, apart from a few precious papers that proved their existence in Myanmar.

Mr. Yunus, the store owner, marshaled his kin. As he left his two-story home, with its spacious garden and surrounding fields, he made sure to lock the door. He would surely be back, he thought.

“I was a rich man in Myanmar,” he said. “I had everything I needed for my family.”

As the soldiers descended on Zammona, Fatema Khatun, the wife of Mr. Amin, one of the men sent to prison, searched frantically for her seven children and thanked Allah that they were all there. She was seven months pregnant with her eighth child. Along their long escape to Bangladesh, a Myanmar soldier grabbed one of her daughters, Sukura Begum, in the forest and raped her, just one horror in what U.N. investigators say was systematized sexual violence. She was 11 years old.

Elsewhere in the village, Morijan, a young mother who goes by one name, searched for her 9-year-old son, Mohammed Omair, who had raced to the west when the artillery began. Two days later, he was found in a rice paddy with a bullet wound through his heart.

At least 10,000 Rohingya were killed by security forces and Rakhine mobs in the immediate aftermath of the 2017 attacks, the U.N. estimated. In Zammona, 10 unarmed men were trussed and killed, then tossed in a mass grave north of the village, said a Myanmar soldier whose testimony, after he ended up in the hands of an enemy militia, marked the first time perpetrators confessed to their crimes. The soldier also said seven Rohingya were shot dead there.

Zammona was wiped from the map, its ruins smoldering for days, visible from a hill in Bangladesh. When he was released from a Myanmar prison four years later, his 16-year sentence commuted, Mr. Rohim returned home before he, too, fled across the border.

“Everything was gone,” he said of Zammona. “I couldn’t recognize anything.”

The Myanmar government soon covered up evidence of the village, building rows of prefab housing on burned earth.

All that was left of Zammona was a large Bodhi tree, sacred to Buddhists because it was the kind under which a prince meditated and gained enlightenment as the Buddha.

In Bangladesh, Mr. Kamal and his family were allotted a tiny shelter with a tarpaulin cover. They could not leave the refugee camps without permission. International assistance allotted each person $12 a month for food, decreased now to $10.

Fatema Khatun’s daughter, who was raped, suffers from debilitating seizures. Three years ago, another daughter, then 18, disappeared for months, then called tearfully from Malaysia, where she said she had been trafficked. She was forced to marry an older man, she said, 50 or 60 years old, she wasn’t sure.

Five years ago, Ms. Khatun’s husband, Mr. Amin, was released from prison a broken man. His kidneys barely work from the beatings. He lies on the floor of their shelter, groaning from an ache that never dissipates. There is no money for painkillers. Occasionally, he repeats the Burmese words he learned in detention: a string of numbers that was his prisoner ID.

“I was supposed to die,” he whispered. “I don’t feel alive.”

On Monday, children crammed into Mr. Kamal’s shelter. His 10-year-old grandson recounted how the boy had been held by the militants, his hands reaching wide to show the size of the blades they brandished. One granddaughter was quiet, but over the hours she leaned against me. Later, she offered a tentative “hello” in English. We practiced sentences.

What is your name? Sadeka Bibi.

How old are you? 13.

Where are you from? Her English faltered. The answer came translated as the block number of her refugee camp. Her mother intervened. Sadeka tried again.

“I am Rohingya,” she said. “I am from Myanmar.”

Mohammed Faisal Arakani contributed reporting.

item.title: Headquarters of Saudi Sovereign Fund Damaged as Houthis Attack Riyadh
item.description:
A skyscraper housing the offices of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund was damaged during an apparent Houthi missile attack on Thursday, underscoring the spiraling costs for the kingdom in its renewed war with the Iran-backed Yemeni militia.

A Times reporter who visited the city’s financial district in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, which is home to the skyscraper, the Public Investment Fund Tower, saw damage to the 80-story building. Black scorch marks were visible around the midsection, and windows on about five floors had been blown out.

Residents of Riyadh, heard a large explosion early Thursday. Soon after, the Saudi authorities reported an attempted Houthi missile attack and said that “falling shrapnel,” which typically results from a missile or drone interception, had caused damage in the city, without specifying where.

The Houthis did not immediately comment on the attack, but they have claimed responsibility for multiple strikes on Riyadh’s financial district in recent weeks, including one that damaged a tower belonging to the Saudi state oil company, Aramco. The Houthis typically say that their attacks are in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.

Saudi Arabia’s roughly $900 billion sovereign wealth fund is the engine of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to overhaul the national economy and reduce dependence on oil. Underpinned by oil revenue, the fund manages high-profile investments around the world, including stakes in major American companies such as Uber and SpaceX, in addition to vast domestic investments in artificial intelligence, manufacturing, sports and entertainment.

The fund and its subsidiaries occupy a lot of the financial district’s real estate, and damaging the headquarters would be a symbolic win for the Houthis.

There was no indication that anyone had been injured in the attack, which happened before the working day had started. Many employees in the financial district have been working from home in recent weeks amid persistent Houthi attacks.

A spokesman for the Public Investment Fund did not respond to a request for comment.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen, have been exchanging escalating attacks for weeks, including on energy facilities and airports. Analysts say that the war is likely to drag on for months. Abdulrahman al-Rashed, a Saudi commentator who is close to the kingdom’s leadership, said in a podcast interview last month that the conflict could last up to two years.

In Yemen, where the Houthis are engaged in heavy fighting with the Saudi-backed government, the impact has been devastating, exacerbating a dire humanitarian crisis. More than 2,200 people have been killed in the fighting over the past few months and nearly 350,000 displaced, according to the World Health Organization.

The two sides have been fighting on and off since 2015, after the Houthis took over the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, routing the internationally recognized Yemeni government and setting off a civil war.

Saudi Arabia led a disastrous bombing campaign to try to restore the Yemeni government to power, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people from violence, hunger and disease. A fragile truce took hold in 2022 but began to unravel in July amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

A full-blown war erupted last month, when the Yemeni government declared a new military campaign against the Houthis, backed by Saudi warplanes.

So far, that campaign has made little headway, and analysts say the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis.

On Sunday, forces backed by Saudi Arabia in southern Yemen said that they were withdrawing from the Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Houthis.

The following day, a royal order by Saudi Arabia replaced the general overseeing operations in Yemen, Fahd al-Salman, with General Fayyad al-Ruwaili, who is also chief of the general staff for the Saudi military.

For Saudi Arabia, the war has threatened to frustrate Prince Mohammed’s hopes of turning the country into a global hub for business and tourism.

A major attack on Riyadh’s airport last month killed at least 14 people and injured more than 300, forcing officials to shut down flights for weeks and cancel a series of high-profile events. Since then, near-daily Houthi attacks have disrupted life across the capital, a city of roughly eight million people.The building that was damaged on Thursday is the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh. It towers over the financial district, a development that also houses banks, multinational companies and luxury apartments.

The Public Investment Fund has played a major role in Prince Mohammed’s efforts to project influence abroad, though financial pressures have pushed Saudi officials to rein in some of their grandest plans.

On Thursday, a large area near the Riyadh tower had been cordoned off, and the neighborhood was mostly empty, save for a handful of security guards and other blue collar workers.

As a group of workers passed the damaged tower, they warned one another to keep their mobile phones in their pockets. The Saudi authorities have threatened to prosecute people who photograph or share information about attacks.

Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from Al Mukalla, Yemen.

item.title: Greenland Pulls Closer to the U.S. — by an Hour
item.description:
For years, Jens Peter Lange has been annoyed about Greenland’s time zone. As a sometime fisherman and hunter in Ilulissat, a Greenlandic city above the Arctic Circle, it was simply disorienting.

“When we head out to go fishing, it’s dark. And when we come back, the sun is coming up,” he said. “It feels weird.”

So Mr. Lange and many other Greenlanders were pleased this month when Greenland’s government, after a heated discussion but an overwhelming vote in favor, decided to shift its time zone an hour earlier.

Greenland, an overseas territory of Denmark, is three hours ahead of Eastern Standard Time and three hours behind Central European Time, which Denmark uses. Starting next October, Greenland will move its clocks back one hour.

Even though closer ties to the United States were not part of the official reason for changing the time zone, and many Greenlanders remain upset about President Trump’s threats to “get” the island, the time shift could facilitate more opportunities for U.S. trade, tourism and investment in Greenland.

It also stands to distance the giant island from Denmark, which colonized Greenland more than 300 years ago and still oversees its defense and much of its foreign policy.

The time zone decision, made on Nov. 12, reverses what Greenland’s leaders did in 2023. Back then, they moved the clocks forward, striving to be closer to Denmark.

The idea was to facilitate more business and communication with Denmark and the rest of Europe. But the move prompted years of complaints, especially from hunters and fishermen who struggled with darker mornings.

And in recent years there has also been rising sentiment in favor of breaking from Denmark. Two opposition parties in Greenland’s Parliament that support fast-tracked independence spearheaded the vote.

Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland’s prime minister, who is relatively pro-Denmark, warned against turning the clocks back again.

He told parliamentarians that doing so would bring “a lasting negative economic impact on society as a whole, including public finances.”

He also said it could lead to fewer and more expensive flights because most come from Denmark, and create problems for Greenland’s health care services, which are heavily dependent on communication with Denmark.

Despite Mr. Nielsen’s warnings, the proposal passed easily, with support from his own party and no votes against it.

In the new time zone, Mr. Lange said, he will work better and sleep better.

“We will go back to our normal biological rhythm,” he said.

The tensions with Mr. Trump have eased since the United States signed a deal in September with Denmark and Greenland to expand the American military presence in Greenland.

But Mr. Trump’s fixation on the Arctic island has spawned a frenzy of American business people prowling for deals in minerals and natural resources. Some were excited by Greenland’s decision to shift time zones.

“I think it’s brilliant,” said Larry Swets, the executive chairman of Greenland Energy Company, a Nasdaq-listed corporation that does oil exploration. “Every extra hour Greenland and the U.S. share in the workday is an hour we can spend building something together.”

Thomas Dans, the chairman of the United States Arctic Research Commission and one of Mr. Trump’s most active allies on Greenland, said it would help facilitate U.S.-Greenlandic trade and tourism.

“The adjustment recognizes Greenland’s positioning within North America,” he said. “It’s a great move.”

item.title: Drone Hits Dutch Embassy Compound in Kyiv, Ukrainian Officials Say
item.description:
The Dutch Embassy in central Kyiv was damaged by a drone on Thursday, Ukrainian officials said, amid a wave of Russian attacks and threats of a dire response to Ukraine’s assault on the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.

It was not immediately clear whether the embassy had been deliberately targeted, and other diplomatic facilities and embassies have been damaged in strikes over the course of the war. Still, the strike came a day after the Russian Embassy in the Netherlands condemned a Dutch defense company’s role in producing missiles used to hit the Kerch Strait Bridge, the Crimean bridge.

Tom Berendsen, the Dutch foreign minister, said a projectile had struck just behind the embassy compound, causing minor damage to the building.

“Fortunately, our colleagues are unharmed,” he said in a statement. “We are investigating exactly what happened.”

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, urged world leaders “to condemn in the strongest terms Russia’s attacks on foreign diplomats.”

Russia’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately comment.

The blast near the embassy was one of many explosions across the Ukrainian capital on Thursday as Russia launched swarms of jet-powered drones at Kyiv, shortly after President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia vowed retaliation for the bridge attacks.

“There will be no negotiations, only retaliation,” Mr. Putin said in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, after meeting with President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping. “Moscow’s response will be far more painful.”

Russia has already opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter, launching daily waves of strikes that have especially targeted Kyiv and its energy system.

The Kremlin’s threats increased, though, amid Ukraine’s latest campaign to sever the Kerch Strait Bridge. That operation began on Monday, with waves of drones and missiles pounding the 12-mile crossing in a bid to sever a vital Russian military supply line.

Alongside domestically produced weapons, Ukrainian forces deployed a low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile made by Destinus, an aerospace and defense company headquartered in the Netherlands.

Destinus said after Tuesday’s strike that seven of its Ruta missiles had penetrated Russian air defenses, helping collapse a large section of the bridge into the sea.

Claire Moses and Maria Varenikova contributed reporting.

item.title: Behind Trump Meeting, Xi and Putin Share a Vision of Usurping U.S. Power
item.description:
At the end of a visit to Moscow more than three years ago, Xi Jinping, the leader of China, uttered a line to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia that has come to define the outlook and actions of the two leaders.

“Right now there are changes, the likes of which we haven’t seen for 100 years, and we are the ones driving these changes together,” he said.

What Mr. Xi meant is this: The two men and their nations are transforming the world order by usurping the role of America as the sole superpower, the undisputed victor of the Cold War.

Both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin share a sense of historical grievance shaped by the expansion and dominance of U.S. power in the more than three decades since the fall of the Soviet Union. But from Mr. Xi’s perspective, that situation is evolving, and, rightly or wrongly, he has embraced a vision of America in terminal decline.

Mr. Xi brazenly used a similar line about historical changes in his opening remarks at a summit with Mr. Putin and President Trump on Thursday. “A transformation not seen in a century is accelerating,” he said at the conclave in Shenzhen, China.

Mr. Xi said the same thing to Mr. Trump when the two met in Beijing in May.

Mr. Putin, for his part, has demonstrated his own eagerness to challenge the United States by continuing his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which he began in February 2022.

The trilateral summit hosted by Mr. Xi in Kylin Villa in Shenzhen was an extraordinary event, since the leaders of the three nations had never met in a formal three-way setting.

Mr. Trump, who has spoken for years with admiration about both autocrats, gushed about being welcomed by the two men. “We are really making history,” he said at their meeting. Earlier, he called each of the men his friend.

But there is no sign that the summit will change the long-running anti-American stance of Mr. Xi or Mr. Putin, nor will Mr. Trump be able to build the same kind of relationship with either of those men that they have with each other.

Mr. Trump has a little more than two years left in his term. Both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin can hold on to power indefinitely, and neither has designated a successor.

“These are two deeply historically minded leaders who view geopolitics through the frame of their own national narratives,” said John Delury, a professor of international politics at the Hopkins-Nanjing Center in China. “They seem to regard themselves as ‘great men in history’ acting on a different plane than mere politicians. Even Trump can be seen as epiphenomenal in their eyes.”

Those two leaders have met more than 40 times. On one occasion, in Tajikistan, Mr. Putin even feted Mr. Xi on his 66th birthday with a champagne toast, cake and Russian ice cream.

More consequentially, China has continued to support Russia through the war in Ukraine. Mr. Xi allows Chinese companies to sell microelectronics and other critical goods to Russian defense companies, helping Mr. Putin continue his invasion despite having lost 400,000 to 500,000 troops in the conflict, U.S. and European officials have said.

China has also bought oil from Russia throughout the war, providing important financial backing to Russia.

R. Nicholas Burns, the ambassador to China in the Biden administration and a former ambassador to NATO, said that he never got any sense of ambivalence from Chinese officials on their support for Russia throughout the war, even though they would insist they were neutral in the conflict.

“It was quite hypocritical,” he said. “I actually think in the course of my time there as ambassador, they doubled down on their support for Russia.”

“It was very transparent that China wanted Russia to emerge stronger and gain an advantage over Ukraine,” he added. “They wanted to see NATO and the United States defeated.”

In Shenzhen, the three leaders discussed the war in Ukraine, which Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin also talked about when they met privately earlier on Thursday. Western intelligence agencies assess that Mr. Putin is not ready to negotiate seriously on a peace settlement, The New York Times reported on Wednesday.

Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin have both been shaped by the breakup of the Soviet Union, which they attribute to American machinations and the weakness of Soviet leaders at the time. In December 2012, the month after he became China’s leader, Mr. Xi gave an important internal Communist Party speech in Guangdong Province in which he said the Soviet Union collapsed because “nobody was man enough to stand up and resist.”

There are other deep historical ties between the two nations that are foundational to the men’s partnership.

Beijing and Moscow fought on the same side in World War II against the Axis nations. Soon afterward, in the Korean War, the two powers sided with North Korea, another communist nation, against American and South Korean forces. That war has not formally ended, and Kim Jong-un, the leader of North Korea — whom Mr. Trump recently said he would like to meet again — has maintained formal security alliances with China and Russia.

Days before Mr. Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he met with Mr. Xi at the Winter Olympics in Beijing, and the two governments announced that their nations had entered into a partnership with “no limits.”

There have been limits, though. Mr. Xi has been concerned about the global economic effects of the war in Ukraine, analysts say, and China generally has avoided sending weapons to Russia. In May, when Mr. Putin went to Beijing after Mr. Trump’s visit, the Russian and Chinese leaders did not finalize an agreement for the construction of a new gas pipeline and energy sales to China from Russia.

At a banquet on Wednesday night in Shenzhen, Mr. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, a former army singer, welcomed Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin and other national leaders who were in town for an Asian economic summit. Mr. Xi had Mr. Trump sit next to him at the head table, while Mr. Putin sat farther away with Ms. Peng. Some people have interpreted that as the Chinese leader possibly snubbing Mr. Putin.

But in two years, Mr. Trump will likely be gone from the world stage, and Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi could be dining together again as leaders of their nations and, in their eyes, great men.

item.title: The Rohingya Crisis Over the Years
item.description:
In 2017, Myanmar’s security forces started a swift, planned and brutal campaign of violence against Rohingya Muslims, an ethnic minority in the country that had already experienced decades of abuse.

Government troops and mobs rampaged through Rohingya communities, killing at least 10,000 people, destroying about 400 villages and carrying out systematized sexual violence, according to investigators with the United Nations.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya. It was the first time a state was held accountable for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The massacres catalyzed the rapid exodus of refugees as Rohingya people fled into neighboring Bangladesh. About 1.2 million of them still crowd precarious camps there.

Reporters and photographers for The New York Times covered that wave of attacks in 2017 as well as the systematic persecution of the Rohingya in the preceding years that had already forced many to flee.

item.title: Life in the Rohingya camps in Bangladesh is becoming more precarious.
item.description:
The Rohingya camps in Bangladesh are the largest refugee settlement in the world. More than 1.2 million refugees from neighboring Myanmar live here, squeezed into tarp shelters that sprawl across steep slopes and denuded forests.

Whatever the outcome of the genocide case at the International Court of Justice on Thursday, I’ve seen firsthand over the past week that life in these camps is unlikely to improve any time soon.

The monsoons bring floods and landslides, the dry season fires that torch the bamboo spines of the shelters. With international assistance drying up, the Rohingya have grown even more precarious. Before, each person received $12 in food aid. That was per month, not per day. Now, because of international funding shortfalls, the monthly stipend has dropped to $10.

I spoke to people who said they hadn’t tasted red meat in years. One man closed his eyes as he recalled the taste of his favorite beef curry.

After President Trump returned to office, Rohingya who were poised to receive refugee status in the United States were abruptly told they were no longer welcome.

Running gun battles between rival militant groups bring terror to the cramped camps. Mothers try to keep their children at home, particularly teenage girls and boys, for fear that they will be kidnapped and forced into sexual slavery or conscripted to fight. As I walked through the camps on Wednesday, the day before the International Court of Justice verdict, two fresh-faced militants sauntered past me, with pistols at their hips.

item.title: After Bridge Attack, Putin Says He Will ‘Not Be Negotiating’ Ukraine Cease-Fire
item.description:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia said on Thursday that “we will not be negotiating” any partial cease-fire with Ukraine after Kyiv’s attacks this week on the only bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

Mr. Putin publicly addressed the strikes, which destroyed a large part of the bridge that carried passenger vehicles, for the first time after a high-profile summit with President Trump and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen, China. He vowed painful Russian retaliation for the attacks.

The Russian leader built the bridge to connect Russia to Crimea in the years after Moscow illegally annexed the peninsula from Ukraine in 2014. It has served as a monument to Russian control over Crimea and to Mr. Putin’s larger imperial ambitions, as well as a crucial transport link for Crimeans.

Mr. Putin said that he had been discussing with his security council the possibility of a cease-fire on shipping in the Black Sea or a halt to strikes on energy infrastructure, but that any such possibility was now off the table.

“After these strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not be negotiating,” Mr. Putin said. He warned that Russia’s retaliation would “be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime has done to the bridge.”

Engineering specialists have said that work to restore the road part of the bridge could take years. Earlier this year, Ukraine tried to cut off Crimea to pressure Moscow to end the war.

Even before the bridge strikes, there was little sign that Mr. Putin was inclined to agree to any cease-fire in the coming weeks. Western intelligence assessments have found that the Russian leader plans to fight in Ukraine at least through the winter.

It was not immediately clear what the Russian leader’s statement meant for a large swap of prisoners of war and perhaps civilian prisoners that Mr. Trump’s special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, helped negotiate at talks in Abu Dhabi last week.

But the announcement immediately dashed meager hopes that talks between Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen would lead to a breakthrough in the Trump administration’s on-again, off-again effort to end the war in Ukraine.

Russia has blamed various Ukrainian attacks for stalled progress on peace talks in the past, including a drone attack that Russia accused Ukraine of launching against Mr. Putin’s lakeside retreat but that Kyiv said never took place.

In his news conference in Shenzhen, Mr. Putin addressed the U.S. request to include European officials in the peace talks, which so far have been limited to Russians, Ukrainians and Americans.

He called insinuations by European officials that Russia was preparing to invade Europe “political diarrhea,” and reiterated his position that stationing Western troops in a postwar Ukraine was a red line that he could not tolerate.

But Mr. Putin also said that Moscow had invited European representatives to Moscow “through diplomatic channels” to clarify their position before determining any role for them in the talks. That statement suggested that the broader U.S.-led peace negotiations could continue, though it was unclear how serious the offer was.

Moscow has in the past rejected various European officials as unacceptable interlocutors, and Mr. Putin on Thursday said it would be impossible to normalize relations “without a change in the political elites in certain European countries.”

Mr. Putin raised doubts about whether he would accept Mr. Trump’s invitation to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami next month. The Russian leader said Mr. Trump had brought up the question twice during their talks in Shenzhen.

No decision has been made yet, Mr. Putin said. But he added that he had to take into account what was happening in Russia, and that it was not always convenient for him to travel abroad. He said a high-level Russian delegation would attend if he did not go.

The Russian leader suggested that if Kyiv wanted to end the war, it should look at what Russia agreed to last year in Anchorage, Alaska, during a summit with Mr. Trump. At the time, Mr. Putin agreed to stop fighting if Ukraine handed over the rest of the eastern Donetsk region, a proposal that Kyiv rejected.

Oleg Matsnev contributed reporting from Munich.

item.title: Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya, Top Global Court Finds
item.description:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a landmark decision years in the making that makes the Southeast Asian nation the first state to be held to account for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ruling covers Myanmar’s deadly military campaign against the Rohingya minority, which killed at least 10,000 people in a few weeks in 2017 and forced three quarters of a million people to flee during that same period. More deaths and expulsions followed.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine state,” Judge Yuji Iwasawa, the president of the I.C.J., said while reading the court’s decision on Thursday. The decision was made by 9 votes to 6.

The decision could have sweeping implications, including for another genocide case before the I.C.J., the United Nations’ highest judicial body: the accusation of genocide by Israel against the people of the Gaza Strip.

A spokeswoman for the government of Myanmar, in the capital Naypyidaw, did not answer a phone call seeking comment after the verdict was handed down. Myanmar authorities have previously disputed the charge.

Among other findings, the court determined that Myanmar had failed to prevent genocide. While it was not found to have incited private people to commit genocide, the court found that it also failed to punish genocide.

“This is a case a decade in the making,” said Juliette McIntyre, a Senior Lecturer in Law at Adelaide University in Australia. “From the point of view of the Rohingya people, who have been waiting, and waiting, and waiting for justice, this is very important.”

Gambia filed suit against Myanmar in 2019 in the court, which is based in The Hague. While the West African country is thousands of miles from Myanmar, international law gives countries the ability to act against genocide anywhere in the world — even if they are not affected.

In the Jamtoli camp of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, people thronged to a public viewing party to watch the hourslong decision, cheering and weeping as the decision was read. Some held signs that said “thank you, Gambia.”

In The Hague, Dawda Jallow, the attorney general for Gambia, welcomed the decision to find Myanmar culpable of the “crime of crimes.” Speaking to journalists on the main staircase of the I.C.J.’s Peace Palace shortly after the ruling was read, he said, “we will stand with the Rohingya until justice is served.”

The violence at the core of the case took place in Myanmar’s far western Rakhine state, starting in 2016 and worsening in 2017. U.N. officials and human rights groups have called it a coordinated, scorched-earth campaign to remove the Rohingya — one that involved killing, wounding and raping, razing villages, and eventually forcing the expulsion of more than a million people to neighboring Bangladesh.

The Rohingya Muslims have a long history of repression in Myanmar. After the nation’s independence from Britain in 1948, they were one of many ethnic groups in the country, which was then known as Burma. But over time, they faced increasing attacks from members of the nation’s Buddhist majority.

A restrictive citizenship law in 1982 effectively rendered most Rohingya stateless. Various Myanmar governments, including a civilian authority led by the Nobel peace laureate Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, have refused to even acknowledge the Rohingya as a legitimate ethnic group, falsely referring to them instead as interlopers from neighboring Bangladesh.

Myanmar’s military called its campaign against the Rohingya “clearance operations.” Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi defended the military at the I.C.J., denying it committed genocide, before her government was deposed by the military and she was imprisoned in 2021. (After the coup, Myanmar descended into a civil war that is still raging.) About 1.2 million Rohingya now live in dire conditions in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh. Following the eruption of Myanmar’s civil war in 2021, much of the Rohingya homeland is now controlled by a milita from the Rakhine ethnic minority, which has also been accused of persecuting Rohingya.

Thursday’s decision hinged on whether Myanmar acted with the specific intent to physically destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group.

The court found that Myanmar took measures to wipe out the Rohingya people, who did constitute a protected ethnic group by the court’s judgment.

The case summary states that, among other atrocities, the court found that “widespread acts of extreme violence were perpetrated by the Myanmar security forces against children in northern Rakhine State,” that “in addition to the extreme hardship of the journey, the Myanmar security forces systematically shot at Rohingya as they were fleeing,” and that “the evidence demonstrates a deliberate, organized process” of destroying Rohingya villages.

“The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the group,” Judge Iwasawa read from the ruling.

The court said that Myanmar must provide restitution — trying to put things back as they were, including through allowing return and reunification — and, where that fails, compensation. But the amount of compensation needed is not yet set, and will be determined in further proceedings.

The court does not have the power to enforce its own rulings, and the U.N. Security Council would need to uphold the decision. Two members of the Security Council, China and Russia, may opt to protect Myanmar. Each provides Myanmar with weapons it now uses to kill civilians in the civil war.

“Concerned governments” should “press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, said in a written statement following the announcement.

Notably, the United States has previously said that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, though that happened during the Biden administration.

“I think that you’re going to see relatively powerful states putting pressure on Myanmar,” said Ms. McIntyre, of Adelaide University. “How much they pay heed to that pressure is a question.”

Thursday’s decision was greeted by some in the international legal community as a sign that justice can still be served on a global stage, even as the Trump administration attacks international bodies. The administration plans to impose sweeping sanctions against another tribunal, the International Criminal Court, which could severely impair the court’s ability to function on a day-to-day basis.

“At a moment when international law and the institutions that uphold it face growing pressure, the Court’s decision reaffirms the vital role they play in establishing truth,” James Goldston, the executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, said in a statement.

For the Rohingya now in Bangladesh, the news was welcome. Yet tragedies continued after 2016 and 2017, the years ruled a genocide by the I.C.J.

Mohammed Yeasin said his wife and sister were killed in a drone attack in August 2024. The perpetrators were not the Myanmar military but the armed group from the Rakhine ethnic minority that shares its homeland with the Rohingya.

“I am happy about the I.C.J.,” he said. “But I don’t know when my sorrows will end.”

Jonathan Wolfe, Marlise Simons and Saikou Jammeh contributed reporting.
